Short answer: Treat the lead Bible teacher (a) first. His repeated, public misuse of God’s name while teaching Scripture by the man the faculty and students look to is the more serious offense because of office, example, and scandal. The coach’s one blowup (b) is gravely wrong in kind (blasphemous cursing) but is less aggravated by public example and official status.

Detailed reasoning from Westminster moral principles and practical counsel

Summary of the two cases
- (a) Lead Bible teacher: ordinally authoritative, admired example, daily careless filler (“oh Lord,” “God knows,” “I swear”) while teaching Scripture to full classrooms, imitated by students.
- (b) Part‑time coach: one profane outburst in an empty gym cursing God’s name, no students present; brushed off when confronted and persists to curse when he thinks no one’s listening.

What the Westminster standards require (briefly)
- The Third Commandment forbids taking the Name of God in vain; the Catechisms and Confession treat all improper uses (careless, common swearing, cursing, perjury, frivolous oaths) as sin. Aggravations include publicness, repetition, position of authority, occasioning others to sin, and a hardened or defiant heart. Restoration and discipline include pastoral admonition, required repentance, and, if necessary, more formal church/office discipline for those in spiritual office.

Aggravating factors and the single most defining feature for each
- (a) Lead Bible teacher — Aggravations:
  - Office and example: ordained, official Bible teacher, model for staff and students.
  - Public and repeated: habitual, day‑by‑day in front of full classrooms while teaching Scripture.
  - Scandal and imitation: children copy adults they respect; harms consciences and reverence for God.
  - Embedded in ministry: misuse occurs in the very context (Bible class) where reverence should be most evident.
  - Single most defining feature: scandalous public example by an ordained spiritual leader while teaching Scripture.
- (b) Part‑time coach — Aggravations:
  - Blasphemous force of language: a genuine profane cursing of God’s name (more intense in wording).
  - Persistence and defiance: he dismissed correction and continues when he thinks no one’s listening.
  - Lesser public scandal: his outburst was alone and not modeled before students, though his ongoing private habit risks future exposure.
  - Single most defining feature: direct, willful profane abuse of God’s name revealing a hardened, unrepentant disposition.

How to weigh them (decisive considerations)
- The Westminster standards weigh not only the intensity of the utterance but also the office, public influence, frequency, and scandal. A leader’s habitual public misuse that habitually bends the consciences of the young and undermines reverence for God is therefore more grievous than a single private outburst, even if that outburst involved stronger language. Conversely, a profane blasphemy shows a heart problem and must not be minimized; persistence and defiance aggravate it and may require firm discipline.

Practical pastoral/administrative guidance (what to do first this week)
- Address (a) first: private pastoral confrontation with the ordained Bible teacher. Use Scripture and Catechism teaching about the Third Commandment, call him to immediate, visible repentance, require concrete corrective steps (stop the filler language, apologize to faculty/students if appropriate, actively teach/restore reverence for God’s name in class, and submit to follow‑up). Because of his office, if he resists or relapses, escalate to formal discipline through the board/church.
- Then address (b): confront the coach, demand repentance, explain why even a private blasphemous outburst is serious. If he persists in private cursing after admonition, impose progressive discipline (written warning, suspension, or termination depending on policy and continued unrepentance). If he shows repentance, require accountability and correction.

Ranking (least to most heinous) and decisive consideration at each step
- Least: (b) — decisive consideration: the sin was committed privately and lacks the public office/imitative scandal that multiplies the harm.
- Most: (a) — decisive consideration: an ordained, public Bible teacher’s habitual, repeated misuse of God’s name in the classroom while teaching Scripture produces scandal and corrupts the flock.

RANKING: b < a

Short answer up front: both are serious sins under the law of God, but on the Westminster moral scheme the deliberate, repeated fraud upon a defenseless widow is the worse. Handle the fraud first and most severely; then address the public puffery—but don’t ignore the latter, because a leader’s public lie is itself an aggravated offense.

Principles from the Westminster Standards I apply here
- The law of God forbids lying and falsehood (the command against bearing false witness) and forbids theft and oppression of the poor. Sin is “any want of conformity unto, or transgression of, the law of God,” and sins are to be judged not only by their kind but by their aggravations (premeditation, habit, malice, breach of trust, causing scandal, and the like).

Brief summary of each case, its aggravations, and its defining feature

(a) The man who willfully spends every Lord’s Day on errands and recreation
- Aggravating features:

  - It manifests contempt for the day God has set apart for worship and rest.
- Single most defining feature:
  - Personal, deliberate, and habitual profanation of the Lord’s Day (a public example of contempt for the Sabbath).

(b) The woman who requires four young singers to attend a Sunday-morning sectional instead of worship
- Aggravating features:
  - She is using her authority to coerce or silence consciences (two are new believers who expressly said they wanted to worship).
  - She is regularly preventing others from attending public worship, contrary to the duty of the day.
  - It threatens the spiritual welfare and conscience of weaker members; it scandalizes the Lord’s Day by making worship impossible for others.
- Single most defining feature:
  - Causing others to be kept from public worship by coercive exercise of authority — an offense against both the Sabbath duty and the duty to protect weak consciences.

Which is worse, and why (decisive consideration)
- The decisive consideration in comparing these two is not merely how bad each person’s own practice is, but whether and how the practice harms other people’s duty to worship. The Shorter Catechism teaches that it is a Sabbath sin to cause others by example or otherwise to profane the day. Causing weaker brethren to be kept from worship is an offense that (1) violates the communal nature of the Lord’s Day, (2) injures the consciences and spiritual development of others, and (3) abuses a position of power to force disobedience. Those features make (b) the more grievous case by Westminster standards.

Practical pastoral/action guidance (what to do first and how)
1. Prioritize (b) first.
   - Immediate pastoral protection: ensure the two new believers are not required to miss their church worship. The board should suspend any requirement that compels attendance at Sunday-morning sectionals that conflict with worship until the matter is resolved.

   - Clear expectations for leaders: the board should set and publish expectations for leaders regarding the Lord’s Day — attendance at worship and refraining from habitual profanation — and the consequences for continued refusal (loss of leadership).
   - If he persists in willful profanation, treat it as a disqualifying behavior for public leadership: remove or suspend him from leadership until repentance is evident.

Short answer from the Westminster moral teaching: you must be honest and just in your dealings, keep your lawful promises, and make restitution for any wrong done. That means you may not quietly withhold the packaging deliverables or keep their deposit while failing to perform what you promised. Why (the principle): the Larger Catechism’s treatment of the eighth commandment teaches that Christians are required to show truth and justice in commerce, to pay just debts and make restitution for what is unjustly kept (i.e. do not defraud your neighbour). The Westminster standard therefore forbids taking advantage of the owners’ trust or language difficulty, and requires faithfulness to written engagements or an honest, agreed renegotiation.

Practical steps — what to do now

6. If you already failed to deliver and they demand completion, be prepared to make restitution (complete the work, hire someone to finish it, or refund in part). Restitution is required if you have caused them measurable loss.

I made a mistake estimating the time. Short answer first: morally, under the teaching of the Westminster Standards you should keep the written bargain unless performance has been rendered impossible; you must be honest and straightforward about the delay; you must not impose a surcharge without the customers’ informed consent; and if the customers cancel you must promptly return the deposit (and make restitution for any loss you caused by wrongful conduct). Practically, you should (1) tell them the truth immediately, (2) offer clear options (honor the contract at $4,200; renegotiate only if they freely agree; or refund the deposit and release them), and (3) do everything reasonable to mitigate your loss (change materials/design, speed the finishing, borrow, etc.) before asking for money.

Why, according to the Westminster Standards
- The Standards ground civil and personal morality in God’s law (especially the commandments requiring truth, justice, and keeping covenants). A lawful promise or covenant is to be kept; breaking an agreed bargain for one’s own convenience is sinful. The eighth commandment’s teaching against stealing and defrauding implies we must not take unjust advantage in commerce; the duty of restitution requires making right any wrongful gain or loss caused by us.
- Oaths, vows and covenants are binding and must be discharged in good conscience where performance is possible. Where a promise cannot be performed (impossibility), the promiser is excused, but that is a narrow category.
- The Standards also require charity and neighbor-love: treat customers fairly, do not use position to coerce them, and be honest about capabilities and timing.

Applied to your case
1. The price: you signed a written order for $4,200. Morally you may not unilaterally demand more; to do so would be breaking a covenant and would be treating them unjustly. You may propose a price adjustment, but it must be by their informed consent. If they refuse, you should either perform for the agreed price or, if you truly cannot perform, allow them to cancel and give a prompt refund of the $2,100 deposit (and, if your conduct earlier misled them in a way that caused extra loss, consider additional restitution).

2. The deposit and “resell” idea: your supplier’s suggestion to present a surcharge and say “refund deposit and resell” treats the deposit as your bargaining chip. That approach is morally questionable unless the contract actually permits unilateral cancellation/resale. If they cancel lawfully, refunding the deposit and reselling is permissible; if you use the threat of deposit forfeiture to coerce payment, that’s a breach of justice.

3. The timeline/finish: you said “I’ll try to have it to you before Thanksgiving if the finish cures in time.” That is an honest, tentative statement, not a fixed promise; you did not commit to Thanksgiving in the written order. But you must not now misrepresent the cure time. Give them an honest status and a revised reasonable completion estimate. If your tentative promise created reasonable expectations and you have been negligent in the care of the work, you may owe some moral compensation for inconvenience; if delay is genuinely due to factors beyond your control, you are not morally guilty of breach of promise for a date you never bound yourself to.

Practical steps to take now
1. Contact the couple immediately, in person or by phone, and follow up in writing: be transparent about the increased material costs, your current position, and the honest status of the finish and delivery date. Apologize for the position and for any inconvenience your earlier quotes created.

2. Offer clear, fair choices:
   - I will honor the written contract at $4,200 and deliver as soon as the finish allows (give a realistic new date and any steps you’ll take to expedite).
   - If they prefer, I can substitute a less expensive wood/design that keeps the price structure similar (explain trade-offs).
   - If they cannot accept either, I will cancel the order and refund the $2,100 deposit promptly so they can pursue other makers.

3. Do not demand a lump-sum surcharge. If they voluntarily accept an increased price, get that agreement in writing.

4. Mitigate your loss where reasonable: look for less expensive lumber alternatives they would accept, speed curing with safe methods, borrow against receivables, or accept a smaller margin. Absorbing part of the increased cost is often the most straightforward way to fulfill a moral promise without bruising the relationship or reputation.

5. If they cancel and you resell to someone else at a higher price, compute honestly whether any profit beyond your earlier loss is due them (typically not — they were not entitled to future gains), but you must not misrepresent facts in the process and you should return the deposit promptly.

A final moral posture
Honor the covenant you made when performance is possible. Be candid and humble; the Standards value truthfulness, justice, and restitution. Bad-faith attempts to coerce more money after the fact are inconsistent with those duties. Practically speaking, humanely explaining the situation and offering fair options often preserves the customer relationship and your reputation—and sometimes customers will voluntarily help shoulder a fair portion of an exceptional increase once treated honestly.

Short answer: Yes — your ordination vows remain morally binding until you are properly released. You should not “ghost” the office or quietly abandon promises. The Westminster Standards teach that Christ institutes church government, that officers are solemnly called to watch for souls and faithfully discharge their duties, and that vows and covenants are to be kept. If you must leave, do it openly, humbly, and by the church’s ordinary order: confess your failure, ask the session to release you, and give a reasonable hand‑off for any practical commitments (including the bookkeeping help you promised).

Why — the Standards in plain terms
- The Westminster Confession teaches that Christ is Head of the Church and that officers are set in the church by his appointment for the good order and edification of the body. Their duties are serious and entrusted to them before God and the congregation.  
- The Catechisms and the Confession treat vows, promises and covenants as morally significant; a public solemn undertaking made before God and the church should not be treated lightly.  
- At the same time, the Standards expect humility, repentance, mutual help, and orderly church discipline and governance. Where an officer becomes unable to serve faithfully (because of sin, weakness, or providential change), the proper response is confession, counsel, and an orderly release — not secret withdrawal.

Practical steps you should take
1) Stop and pray; acknowledge honestly before God that you have not been faithful and that you are weary and frustrated. Seek pastoral counsel and help for burnout. The pastoral relationship exists to carry burdens like this.  
2) Ask for a private meeting with the pastor and/or the session. Be frank: confess your failure to fulfil the office as you intended, explain the reasons (burnout, brokenness, conflict with the pastor), and state what you now discern is needed (rest + restoration and a return to service, or release from the office). This gives them opportunity to shepherd you and to restore order in the church.  
3) If you need to step down, request formal release from the session (or follow whatever ecclesiastical procedure your denomination uses). Do not simply stop showing up; an orderly resignation honors your vow and protects the church. Offer a reasonable transition period so responsibilities aren’t abruptly abandoned.  
4) For the bookkeeping promise: even if you never signed as treasurer, you did give a promise (“help look at the books”). That is a moral obligation. Either fulfill that promise, or if you cannot, explain the situation to the deacons, apologize for the delay, and provide a plan: a firm short deadline when you will do the work, or help identify and hand off to someone else, or provide the records and training so they can secure competent help. Don’t leave the church’s finances unattended.  
5) If relational conflict with the pastor is a factor and cannot be resolved in session, follow the church’s higher court / presbytery procedures for mediation or examination (the Standards require orderly recourse when internal reconciliation fails).  
6) Make restitution where needed: confess to those you’ve neglected, ask forgiveness, and be available to aid transition. That’s part of keeping faith with the flock you promised to serve.

Suggested tone and content for what you say (examples)
- To session/pastor (in person and followed by brief written note): “I need to confess that I have not served the office as I promised at my ordination. I have been burned out and bitter, and I’m sorry. I need counsel and relief. I ask the session’s help to discern whether I should be restored after rest and counsel or be formally released from my office. I will cooperate in a timely handover of any duties.”  
- To the deacons about the bookkeeping promise: “I’m sorry I have not followed through on my offer to help with the books. I am willing to (a) come in on [two dates] to review the records, or (b) if the deacons prefer, help identify someone else to do it and give them access/hand‑off materials. Please let me know what you need and forgive my delay.”  

A few pastoral cautions
- Don’t use the session’s failure or others’ neglect as your primary excuse for ghosting. Even if others are lax, that does not free you from your vow. But it can be part of your explanation to the session as you seek release or restoration.  
- Burnout is real. The session should help you with rest and restoration; stepping down may be the right thing, provided it’s done openly and responsibly.  
- If you truly repent, there is grace: confess, seek forgiveness, and make amends. The Standards emphasize both the binding nature of vows and the duty of mutual restoration.

If you want, I can:
- Draft a short resignation/release request you can use with your session, and a brief note to the deacons about the bookkeeping; or  
- Outline an honest script for your meeting with the pastor/session to make the conversation less awkward.

Short answer up front: as a Christian bound by the teaching of the Westminster Standards, you should treat the contract as morally binding and not use a vague force‑majeure clause as a pretext to exploit the cafe. Increased cost alone is normally not "impossibility" that releases you; the Standards require truthfulness in oaths and faithfulness in promises, and condemn profiting by oppressing a neighbor. Practically, be honest, seek a fair, charitable re‑negotiation if necessary, or else honor the price for the remaining two months and look for other ways to manage the loss.

Why — the doctrinal basis
- The Westminster Confession and Catechisms consistently affirm the duty of Christians to keep vows, oaths, promises and covenants (see the Confession’s treatment of oaths and vows and the Catechisms’ teaching about truth, justice and mercy). A lawful promise made should be performed; God is truth and requires faithfulness in our dealings.
- The Standards also require love and justice toward our neighbour and condemn oppression for gain. Deliberately invoking a contractual loophole to abandon a struggling neighbor for greater profit would be unjust and uncharitable.
- Where performance is truly made impossible (not merely more expensive) by unforeseen events, there may be legitimate grounds for release; but ordinary increased cost is generally the risk of business and does not remove the moral duty to keep one’s word.

What that means for your situation (practical steps)
1) Read the contract carefully and get legal advice about the force‑majeure language and your legal obligations. Legal release and moral right are related but not identical; law may allow something that conscience should not.
2) If there is a genuine, clear-cut impossibility of performance (for example, total inability to obtain beans at all), proceed with frank notice, help the café find alternatives, and offer compensation where owed. If the clause only covers events that have not occurred, don’t manufacture an excuse.
3) If the contract merely leaves you with much higher cost, treat that as a foreseeable business risk you accepted when you locked the price. Ethically you should honor the $11.50 for the remaining two months if you can reasonably do so.
4) Before assuming you must eat the loss, be transparent with the café owner. Tell her the cost situation, explain your tight margin, and propose options such as:
   - Keeping the $11.50 for the remainder but asking for a modest phased increase thereafter;
   - Reducing weekly volume or changing grind/packaging to lower your cost to supply her at an affordable price;
   - Temporarily splitting the increase for a month while you seek other ways to cover the loss; or
   - If you truly cannot continue, give generous notice and assistance in transition (help her find another roaster or supply alternative) and, if possible, offer some compensation for disruption.
5) Avoid a public or private posture of “maximize at all costs.” Your witness, reputation, and conscience matter. If you break the contract for profit, accept that you must repent and, if you harmed her, make restitution and public acknowledgement.
6) On the business side, simultaneously look for ways to manage your costs: renegotiate with suppliers, raise prices for new accounts, trim other expenses, or temporarily reallocate inventory. You should steward your business, but stewardship is not a license to break faith with a vulnerable neighbor.

A final pastoral note
The Standards call Christians to be faithful in speech and dealings and to practice mercy. If honoring the agreement causes you severe hardship that imperils your ability to care for your own dependents, that changes the moral calculus — the need to provide for one’s household is also a biblical duty — but even then, the right course is honesty, negotiation, and generous notice, not opportunistic coercion. Take counsel from your church elders as you decide, and pray for wisdom.

Short answer: Do not quietly treat your signed commitment as optional. Under the plain moral teaching of the Westminster Standards, a public, written promise to serve your congregation is a binding duty you should keep unless you are legitimately released by the church’s officers or there is an unavoidable, moral necessity. Before you decide to go, be transparent with the committee and the elders, ask for a formal release if one is appropriate, and exhaust every possible way to make the Christmas music work without abandoning the people who have relied on you.

Why, on the Standards
- The Westminster Confession and Catechisms ground obedience in God’s law: our word and vows are not to be trifled with. Public promises and undertakings—especially those made to the church and in service of public worship—carry moral force. Keeping covenants and promises is repeatedly treated as duty (the Standards draw on Scripture in insisting on faithfulness).  
- The Standards also put public worship and the edification of the congregation at the center of a Christian’s duty. Using gifts for God’s glory in the ordinary life of the local church is a primary stewardship.  
- Where a promise cannot be kept, the Standards require honest confession, restitution where possible, and submission to church order (seek pastoral/elderly oversight).

Practical counsel (concrete steps)
1. Stop the “quiet renegade” plan. Don’t change the arrangement without telling the committee, the choir, and the elders. Secretly breaking a written commitment is the kind of thing the Standards would call morally wrong (selfish dissembling) unless you have been formally excused.  
2. Talk with the music committee and the session/elders immediately and openly. Explain the offer, its dates, and why it conflicts. Ask them to advise and, if they judge it right, to release you from part or all of the commitment. Their blessing (or withholding it) matters morally and pastorally.  
3. Explore every alternative before assuming you must be absent:  
   - Can the touring group shift one date, or can you attend part of the evening/service?  
   - Can you prepare the choir beforehand so an associate, accompanist, or rehearsal track can lead that piece at dress rehearsal and on the Eve? (Record a clear conducting video, give detailed cues, rehearse the substitute.)  
   - Can you conduct at the earlier service (if there are multiple services) and make arrangements for the later one?  
4. If the committee/elders release you after prayerful consideration, accept that release gratefully and help make excellent contingency plans for the choir and congregation (so you do not leave them worse off). If they do not release you, you should keep your commitment.  
5. If, after consulting the officers and conscience, you go anyway without release and that choice harms the congregation or choir reliance, then the Standards require confession and restitution: acknowledge the breach to those affected, make practical amends (help find and prepare a substitute, offer compensation for expenses or extra work), and repent before God and the church.  
6. Learn from this to avoid similar conflicts: be cautious about making public, written commitments if you know you may receive high-pressure offers; build backup plans and train at least one competent deputy.

A pastoral note
This is a tempting opportunity and a legitimate honor. The Standards do not forbid lawful and honorable secular opportunities; they do insist that we serve God faithfully, keep our word, and submit to the church’s care. Let charity for your choir and fidelity to your promise guide you. If the elders judge that the greater godly good is served by letting you go, go with their blessing and help the church through the transition; if they judge you should stay, honor the congregation’s reliance on you. Either way, be honest and repair any harm you cause.

Friday Night Charter — A Covenant of Brothers

Preamble
We gather each Friday as friends, for fellowship, food, cigars, and fun. This charter is our short, serious agreement: warm in spirit, plain in duty. We bind ourselves to protect one another’s welfare, peace, and reputation. We intend this to be brotherly, not legalistic — but we mean it.

1) Buy-in and play
- The cash buy-in is $20. Keep it small; if you can’t afford $20, come anyway — you’ll sit out or play house money. No one plays with money they can’t spare. We will call someone on it if their play threatens their family or livelihood and help them step away if needed.

2) Danny’s nights — no cards
- Danny is 14 months out from gambling addiction and has told us plainly that cards are a live snare for him. When Danny is here, there are no card games. We’ll play dominoes, board games, or just share cigars and talk. Grumbling is human; pressuring or undermining the decision is not. Danny’s recovery is more important than any hand.

3) Conscience, freedom, and responsibility
- We will not turn fellowship into a tribunal of conscience. Poker is not treated here as a sin, and we won’t impose legalistic rules on one another. At the same time, we will not coerce anyone to do what they judge wrong. If a brother conscientiously chooses to sit out or cut back, we will receive that choice with respect and care — we will not demand a public apology or explanation. If there is confusion or strain in the group about someone’s choices, we’ll handle it privately and pastorally, not by shaming or public pressure.

4) Business deals, cars, and Danny
- We will not ask or pressure Danny to broker deals that re-expose him to old, unhealthy relationships or illegal activity. His recovery and safety take precedence. If a member needs help finding a reliable used car or negotiating a sale, we will help as a group through lawful, above-board means: pooled research, sharing vetted leads, or negotiating together. If Danny independently offers to help and it is a sober, voluntary choice made without pressure, that’s his decision — but we will not structure deals intended to leverage his past debt or to put him at risk. We will refuse to involve or encourage contact with anyone known to operate illegally.

5) Confidentiality
- What’s said at the table stays at the table. We don’t repeat a man’s business around town, ridicule private struggles, or spread gossip. If something shared requires intervention (harm to self or others, crime in progress), we will act responsibly and, where necessary, involve the right authorities or loved ones.

6) Hosting and hospitality
- We rotate hosts and snack duties on a fair schedule. The host provides the space and sets basic house expectations (clean-up, smoking area, noise). If a hosting night needs to deviate (no smoking, special guest, etc.) the host will announce it ahead of time and we’ll adapt. Hosts may ask for a small contribution toward supplies; nothing should be a burden.

Enforcement and pastoral care
- This is a covenant among brothers, not a court. If someone repeatedly violates the spirit or letter of this charter, we will first speak to him privately and seek reconciliation. Repeated, unresolved breaches that harm the group’s safety or integrity may lead to temporary suspension from nights until the matter is resolved.

Why these rules
- We’re together to enjoy friendship, not to endanger livelihoods, exploit weaknesses, or enforce conscience. We’ll guard each other’s hearts, reputations, and recovery with charity, courage, and plain speech.

Signatures
By signing below, I commit to these duties in good faith, for the good of the fellowship and the good of each brother.

Host (me): ____________________   Date: ___________

Danny: _______________________   Date: ___________

[space for other regulars to sign]

Kingdom Business Creed for [Lot Name]
Under the lordship of Jesus Christ, by the rule of Scripture and in the spirit of faithful stewardship taught in our Confession, I covenant to run this business as a servant of the King. This framed pledge shall guide my daily dealings and stand as a public witness of my conscience before God and neighbor.

1. Price as Stewardship
I will set my prices by honest appraisal of market and value. I will read each deal, be shrewd in business, and charge what the car is worth. When a buyer knows the market I will not be ashamed to take the gain of my skill; when a buyer pays full sticker without haggling I will treat that price as legitimate and not volunteer an arbitrary discount. I will not hide behind false modesty about lawful profit; honest gain from honest labor is a good and clean thing.

2. Truth and Disclosure
When selling "as‑is, no warranty" I will make the written terms plain and conspicuous. I will never knowingly conceal material defects or engage in deceptive silence about faults I actually know. For latent or hard‑to‑detect problems I will document what I know and, where law or conscience requires, disclose them; where I sell as‑is I will do so honestly, not by design to defraud. I will honor the principle that a man ought not to oppress his neighbor by fraud or falsehood.

3. Industry, Profit, and Conscience
I reject guilt for pursuing a lean, disciplined, and prosperous lot. I affirm that hard work, prudent ambition, and lawful profit are not vices but callings to glorify God and provide for family, employees, and the needy. I will guard my heart against covetousness and measure success by faithfulness, not mere accumulation.

4. Firstfruits and Giving
Before I withdraw a dollar, I will give the first tenth of this month's net to the local church as my covenantal act of worship and trust. I commit to generous, regular giving beyond this tithe as needs and opportunities arise.

5. A Voluntary Rule on Debt
As a personal and binding rule of conscience, I will not incur business loans for expansion. I choose a debt‑free path as my discipline and testimony that the Lord is my provider. This is my voluntary vow, made under God and subject to Scripture and pastoral oversight; I will revisit it only if conscience, Scripture, and godly counsel require.

6. Covenants and Community
I will keep every written warranty I give. I will not slander or badmouth the dealer across town; rather I will compete fairly, speak truthfully, and promote the good of the trade. I will treat employees, customers, and competitors with justice, fidelity, and charity.

Final Charge
I sign this creed before God, to be read and obeyed as an act of worship. If I fail, I submit to correction, restitution where required, and the discipline of the community. May all profit, prudence, and promise here made be used to glorify Christ, advance his kingdom, and serve my neighbor in love.

Household Covenant of [Family Name]
Home Altar Kit — Nightly Covenant Litany

Preface
We enter this covenant before the one true God — Father, Son, and Holy Spirit — and before one another. We acknowledge that salvation, blessing, and protection come only from God through Jesus Christ. The items in this box (the cornerstone and the covenant oil) are outward signs and reminders appointed to strengthen our faith and duty; they are not small talismans, nor do they confer blessing in themselves. We promise by God’s grace to use these means as instruments of worship, teaching, and dependence upon the Lord, in accordance with Holy Scripture.

A Solemn Covenant
We, the members of this household, bind ourselves this day to gather at our home altar each evening for the order below. We make this vow before God and one another, asking God’s help to keep it faithfully.

Nightly Order (to be observed each evening)
1. Scripture and Prayer
- One household reader reads a short passage of Scripture aloud (a psalm, a gospel text, or another suitable portion).
- The family then pauses a moment to give thanks and to pray together, confessing sin, praising God, and asking for grace for the night.

2. The Cornerstone (sign and testimony)
- Each member places a hand upon the boxed “anointed cornerstone.”
- Together we say: “As a sign before God, we place our hands upon this cornerstone and covenant to build our home upon the Lord Jesus Christ, the living Cornerstone. We pray that, by God’s mercy, His favor and protection rest upon all who dwell here.” 
- (Note: this is spoken as a covenantal prayer and testimony of trust in God — not as a declaration that the stone itself possesses power.)

3. Parental Blessing
- The parents lay hands upon each child in turn and speak a blessing. A suggested blessing is:
  “May the Lord bless you and keep you; may His face shine upon you and give you peace (Numbers 6:24–26). May you grow in the grace and knowledge of Christ, walking aright before God and men.”
- Parents may add scriptural or personal exhortations and prayers for the child’s growth in grace.

4. Psalm or Hymn
- The family sings a psalm or hymn together (sung or read aloud if singing is not possible). Singing the Psalms is especially encouraged as God’s own prayer-book.

5. Monthly Renewal of the Sign
- Once each month, the parents place one drop of the covenant oil on the stone while the family prays: “O Lord, renew the covenant of our household; sanctify and strengthen us to walk in Your ways.” 
- This oil is a sign of solemn dedication and petition. We affirm again that the oil itself does not grant blessing; we pray to God alone.

Concluding Prayer and Amen
- Close with a short prayer asking God to establish this covenant in mercy and to enable faithfulness, and conclude with the Lord’s Prayer and “Amen.”

A Final Affirmation (to be signed)
We, the undersigned, do solemnly vow before God and one another to observe the nightly practices described above, to seek the Lord together, to instruct and nurture one another in the faith, and to use the stone and the oil only as signs that point us to Christ. We renounce any superstition or trust in outward things apart from the living God, and we seek God’s help to keep this covenant in sincerity and love.

Signed on this day, ____________ (date)

Father/Head: __________________________
Mother/Head: _________________________
Child: _______________________________
Child: _______________________________
(Additional lines as needed)

Practical Notes (keep on the altar)
- Use the included oil sparingly and keep away from flames. For safety, do not ingest.
- If you are in doubt about any use of the stone or oil, consult your pastor. This kit is designed to cultivate household worship and parental responsibility, not to replace the ordinary means of grace given by Christ in Word and Sacraments nor the oversight of the church.

We invite you to enter this covenant in the fear of the Lord, trusting in His faithfulness alone. May this household be built upon Christ the Cornerstone. Amen.

I have prepared a warm but binding set of Sunday Worship Enhancement Standards for adoption by the Session, drafted so as to be faithful to our church’s subscription to the Westminster Standards. Where a requested practice would depart from the Confession and Catechisms, I have not included it in the form proposed; instead I have set forth a confessional and pastorally helpful alternative the Session may lawfully bind the congregation to. Below is the proposed text for Session action, followed by a brief confessional rationale.

Sunday Worship Enhancement Standards
Preamble
We, the Session of [Church Name], being bound to keep the worship of God in all things according to His Word and the Westminster Standards to which this Session and congregation subscribe, adopt these Standards to promote reverence, order, and the faithful administration of the means of grace in our weekly assemblies. These Standards are binding upon all corporate Sunday services of this congregation and are to be observed until altered by Session.

Article I — Time, Duration, and Order
1.1 Services shall begin at 10:30 a.m. on the Lord’s Day and shall be conducted so as to conclude within seventy-five (75) minutes unless Session grants a particular exception.
1.2 An order of service (liturgy) shall be prepared and printed weekly and shall be followed as printed for that Lord’s Day. Deviations from the printed order are permitted only by prior approval of the Worship Planning Team and Session.
1.3 The printed order shall set forth the elements of worship, their sequence, and the time allotments so that the whole congregation may worship with reverence and understanding.

Article II — Stations of Reflection (Corporate Pastoral Aid)
2.1 To assist private and corporate devotion within the bounds of Scripture, Session authorizes an eight (8) minute segment called “Stations of Reflection.” This segment shall be pastoral, optional, and Scripturally grounded.
2.2 Four stations may be placed in the nave as pastoral aids. Each station shall contain only:
  a) a clearly printed Scripture passage or short Scripture-based meditation card;
  b) a brief written prayer or prayer prompt;
  c) a notice that the station is optional and that worshippers may remain in their seats if they prefer.
2.3 No object at any station shall be treated or taught to be sacramental or to convey grace apart from Christ and His Word. The use of oil, water, incense, candles as sacramental media, holy water, anointing in corporate worship, processional incense, relics, or any element presented as possessing intrinsic spiritual efficacy is expressly prohibited during the Stations of Reflection.
2.4 The stated purpose of the Stations of Reflection is pastoral: to invite Scripture-focused silent prayer and reflection, directing hearts by the Word to Christ and to prayer. Under no circumstance shall these stations be taught or presented as “opening the heart to receive grace” in any quasi-sacramental or magical sense; instruction shall make plain that grace is given by Christ through the Holy Spirit, especially by the proclaimed Word and the sacraments duly administered.

Article III — Annual Covenant Renewal Service (Church Anniversary)
3.1 On the church’s anniversary the congregation shall observe an Annual Covenant Renewal Service, designed to focus the people on the gospel, thankful remembrance, exhortation, and renewal of godly vows and commitments.
3.2 The Covenant Renewal Service may include public Scripture reading, exhortation, prayer of dedication, corporate confession, and an invitation for members to renew covenantal commitments verbally or by a printed responsive form. Any symbolic action must be explicitly non-sacramental, voluntary, and explicitly described as symbolic and pastoral.
3.3 The Session forbids any annual rite that requires members to touch oil, water, or other material tokens as a condition of renewal, or any formula described as a binding decree that effects spiritual reality apart from the Word and the Spirit. Public renewal is a solemn act of covenantal witness, not a new sacrament or magical rite.

Article IV — Preaching
4.1 The sermon shall ordinarily be placed in the final third of the service to prepare the congregation for benediction and dismissal.
4.2 Preaching time shall not exceed twenty-five (25) minutes except by the permission of the Worship Planning Team and with Session oversight. Preachers shall labor to be faithful, biblical, and concise; sermons must expound Scripture and apply it to the lives of the people.

Article V — Music
5.1 Sung worship in the gathered congregation shall be drawn from the church’s approved psalter-and-hymn list. The worship-leading team shall ensure that congregational singing remains central and that any additional musical offerings are consonant with the Regulative Principle and approved repertoire.
5.2 Introduction of texts or tunes not on the approved list requires Session approval.

Article VI — Oversight, Training, and Compliance
6.1 The Worship Planning Team shall ensure that every element of the Sunday liturgy conforms to these Standards and to the Westminster Standards. The Worship Planning Team shall train leaders and provide the printed order to the Session for review when changes are proposed.
6.2 These Standards are binding. Any proposed element not plainly permitted here must be submitted in writing to Session for prior approval. The Session shall remove or correct unauthorized practices observed in corporate worship.

Effective Date and Review
These Standards take effect upon adoption by the Session and shall be reviewed at least annually. Changes require Session action.

Confessional Rationale (brief)
- The Westminster Confession (ch. 21) and the teaching of the Catechisms uphold the Regulative Principle of worship: the acceptable way of worshipping God is instituted by Himself through Scripture and is therefore limited to those elements appointed in His Word. Novel rites, ceremonies, or practices not instituted by Christ and His apostles are disallowed.
- The sacraments ordained by Christ and commanded in Scripture are baptism and the Lord’s Supper (WCF ch. 27). No other acts are to be treated as sacraments or as conveying grace ex opere operato; therefore corporate uses of anointing oil, “holy water,” incense, or other ritual objects as means of grace are not permissible as regular parts of our worship.
- Pastoral aids that point worshippers to Scripture and prayer are allowable so long as they are explicitly non-sacramental, optional, and employed under Session oversight. The Stations of Reflection are so limited and framed.
- Annual covenantal renewal is a long-standing Reformed practice when properly conducted under Scripture and Session oversight; it must not be made into a novel sacrament or a quasi-magical “decree.”

If the Session desires, I will place this text on the next Session agenda for adoption; I can also prepare a short explanatory leaflet for members explaining the Stations of Reflection and the Covenant Renewal Service in language that is pastoral and confessional.

If you wish, I can also prepare the weekly order-of-service template and sample Station meditation cards that conform strictly to the Standards above.

Short answer, by the Westminster Standards: both elders are partly right and partly wrong. The Standards allow using a church calendar as a pastoral, optional aid in discipleship; they forbid imposing uncommanded holy days or rites as required worship of conscience. Therefore you may adopt seasons and recommended devotions as voluntary, prudential practices for growth, but you may not bind them on the conscience or require them as part of the church’s worship.

Why (Confessional basis)
- The regulative principle of worship in the Confession (chapter 21) requires that the elements and manner of public worship be founded on God’s revealed will. Worship must not be invented by men and imposed as required worship. That rule is aimed precisely at preventing the church from commanding “holy days” and rites that Scripture does not appoint.
- The Confession also affirms Christian liberty and that God alone is Lord of the conscience (WCF ch. 20). The church must not compel believers in matters of worship or religion contrary to Scripture.
- At the same time, the Confession recognizes that the church may order the circumstances of worship (times, decency and order) and may, by wise pastoral discretion, commend fasting, thanksgiving, and other devotional exercises. Historically the Standards allow occasional public fasts or thanksgivings when providence calls for them; they do not authorize establishing new commanded festivals or holy days as binding.

How that applies to the specific proposals
- Teaching the congregation about Advent, Lent, Maundy Thursday, etc., as seasons that can help Christians focus on Christ, repentance, and discipleship is a lawful pastoral practice if presented as optional, edifying, and subordinate to Scripture. That is the “lawful circumstance” side.
- Making those seasons “spiritually obligatory” — i.e., binding them on the conscience, requiring observance, imposing new rites as part of the church’s worship — would conflict with WCF 21 and WCF 20. That is what the Confession forbids.
- Specific practices that strongly resemble sacramental or Romish rites (for example, liturgical imposition of ashes as a required act of worship, or treating saints’ days as days of mediatorial invocation or required observance) are especially to be avoided. Commemorating exemplary Christians for instruction is permissible; invoking saints or elevating commemorations to required holy days is not.

Practical ruling and recommended policy for the session
1. Do not adopt or require any new “holy day” or rite as mandatory worship. Vote that no calendar observance will be imposed on conscience or made part of the church’s required worship life.
2. You may adopt a church calendar as a pastoral tool: teach, organize teaching series, encourage voluntary devotional practices, and observe seasons like Advent and Lent liturgically/educationally so long as participation is clearly voluntary and nothing done claims to be a commanded act of worship.
3. Prohibit any practice that communicates that nonparticipation is sinful or disobedient; make clear in bulletins/announcements that these are recommended, not required.
4. Avoid rites that would appear to be sacramental or involve invocation of the dead. If you use symbolic acts (e.g., optional imposition of ashes), make them explicitly voluntary, non-sacramental, and theologically explained so they cannot be taken as imposed worship or a means of grace apart from the Word and sacraments.
5. Provide teaching to the congregation explaining the Bible and Confession’s principles: why we keep the Lord’s Day, what the church may do in wisdom, and why we will not bind uncommanded holy days.
6. If contention remains, consider a clear session statement or rubric (circulated in advance) and a congregational vote on the calendar-policy (not on adoption of particular devotional practices). Keep the presbytery informed if there is a complaint or appeal.

Suggested short ruling language you can read to the congregation
“As a session subscribing to the Westminster Standards, we judge that using the historic church year (Advent, Lent, Holy Week, etc.) as a teaching and devotional aid is permissible. However, no such observance shall be imposed by the church as a required holy day or act of worship, nor shall any rite not appointed in Scripture be required of the conscience. Participation in any calendar observance is voluntary, and the Lord’s Day and Scripture alone remain normatively authoritative for the church’s worship.”

If you want, I can draft a short statement for your bulletin or a sample session minute that embodies the ruling and cites the relevant Confession paragraphs.

Thank you — I’ve thought this through both practically and from the perspective of the Christian principles I teach and live by (as summarized in the Westminster Standards: the moral law rightly governs life, but Christian liberty forbids imposing non‑essential practices as tests of conscience). Below is the Team Culture & Conduct Code I will hand the committee this week. It is warm, covenantal, and binding for participation; it keeps safety, fairness, and the spiritual convictions of families in balance. After the code I list explicitly what I will not put in and why, and what I will keep and enforce.

Team Culture & Conduct Code — Community United Soccer (Co‑Ed, ages 13–16)

Purpose
We play to develop skill, character, and community. Our aim is excellence on the field, respect off it, and a team culture shaped by Christian love: humility, truthfulness, self‑control, and service (Matt. 22:37–40; WCF chap. 19 & 20: moral law guides life; Christian liberty governs indifferent matters). This Code is a covenant among players, families, and coaches to keep practices and games safe, welcoming, and productive.

Commitment
By participating, players and a parent/guardian agree to the expectations below. This Code applies to practices, games, team travel, team chats, and team‑sponsored events.

Core Expectations (I will enforce)
1. Punctuality and Commitment
- Players will make a reasonable effort to attend practices and games on time and notify the coach in advance of absences. Repeated unexplained absences may affect playing opportunities.

2. Respect and Sportsmanship
- All players will treat coaches, referees, opponents, teammates, and volunteers with courtesy and respect. Abusive language, taunting, or unsportsmanlike conduct is not permitted.

3. Appropriate Athletic Attire
- Players will wear the league/team uniform for games and appropriate athletic clothing for practice. Clothing must be safe for play (no loose jewelry, shoes tied). The team will maintain a modesty standard applied equally to all players: athletic shorts and shirts appropriate for participation and safety. The league uniform policy remains in force.

4. Safety and Supervised Transport
- Parents/guardians must provide or arrange safe transport to and from practices and games. For team‑organized travel, parents must provide permission. Drivers must be licensed and carry appropriate insurance. Where possible, we encourage two‑adult carpools or parental consent when a single adult driver is transporting a player. (See Transportation clause below for details.)

5. Music & Media
- Music played at practices and team events will be family‑friendly, non‑explicit, and chosen to promote a positive practice environment. The coach will select or approve playlists; parents may raise concerns privately with the coach.

6. Leadership, Playing Time, and Captaincy
- Playing time and leadership roles (including captaincy or armbands) are awarded by the coach based on attendance, attitude, effort, skill development, leadership, and what is best for team competitiveness and growth. Financial support, donor status, or parental influence will not determine playing time or leadership. Commitments such as extra training, consistent attendance, and demonstrated leadership will be recognized.

7. Inclusion and Non‑Shaming
- No player will be shamed, benched, or otherwise disadvantaged because they cannot afford gear or have hand‑me‑downs. If a player comes without proper uniform, the coach will work with the family and the league to provide a loaner or accommodate the player so they can participate.

8. Parent Communication
- Parents will raise concerns directly and privately with the coach first. Public campaigning through team chats, social media, or pressuring players or families is not permitted. If concerns remain unresolved, bring them to the Coaching Committee/Board by the established grievance process.

9. Discipline
- Minor infractions will receive a verbal warning and a discussion. Repeated or serious violations (fighting, abuse, safety risks) may result in suspension or removal from the team after review by the coach and the Committee. Discipline aims at restoration, not punishment.

10. Optional Devotions & Voluntary Commitments
- The coach may offer brief, voluntary devotional times or prayers at the start or end of practice. Participation is strictly voluntary. No player will be required to participate in religious activities as a condition of playing.

Transportation (details)
- The team does not arrange unsupervised carpools. Parents may organize carpools among themselves. If a parent requests the coach to help coordinate carpools, the coach will share parents’ contact info only with permission. For safety, when an adult of the opposite sex is transporting a minor, parents are encouraged to consent in writing; alternative arrangements will be made if a parent prefers. The coach will follow league and organizational child‑safety policies.

Signatures
- Players and a parent/guardian sign to indicate they have read and will abide by this Code. Signing is consent to the behavioral expectations and the grievance/discipline process, not a religious pledge.

What I will not require or enforce (explicitly)
- I will not require a religious "purity pledge" as a condition of participation. The Westminster Standards teach that true religion is a matter of the heart and faith; making such a pledge mandatory risks legalism and coerced conscience (WCF chap. 20). Families who wish to make private religious commitments may do so personally or as a voluntary group activity, but it will not be a team requirement.
- I will not single out girls for stricter clothing rules than boys. Modesty standards apply equally to all genders. Requiring “only knee‑length shorts for girls” as a special rule is discriminatory and inconsistent with our emphasis on equal treatment and safety.
- I will not prohibit all secular music at practice. Music used must be family‑friendly. A blanket ban is a needless restriction of Christian liberty in indifferent things; the coach will use discretion to maintain a positive environment.
- I will not forbid mixed‑gender carpools as an absolute rule. I will require parental consent and follow child‑safety best practices; parents may choose not to participate in mixed carpools and are free to organize same‑gender transportation.

What I will keep and enforce (explicitly)
- The league’s existing rules on respectful language, appropriate athletic attire (applied fairly), and supervised transport will remain in force.
- Expectations on punctuality, attendance, respect for refs/opponents, coach‑determined playing time based on fair criteria, and the parent communication clause will be enforced.
- The inclusion clause guaranteeing no shaming or penalty for inability to afford gear will be enforced; I will arrange loaner uniforms or alternate solutions so every player can participate.
- The rule that parents must raise concerns directly with the coach (not through public campaigning) will be enforced; repeated violation may lead to escalation to the Committee.

Why these choices (brief theological and practical rationale)
- Scripture calls us to pursue holiness and true repentance, but also warns against binding consciences with non‑essentials (the Westminster Standards teach the moral law is binding but Christians enjoy liberty in indifferent matters). Making personal devotional practices or non‑essential traditions a team requirement risks legalism and harms unity (WCF ch. 20–21). At the same time, the moral law’s demands (truthfulness, respect, modesty expressed as love for neighbor) are properly enforced in a team setting to protect safety and community.

A Christian Covenant of Partnership
for [Company Name], LLC
Preamble
We, the undersigned, believers in the Lord Jesus Christ and members of [congregation or church name, optional], acknowledging God’s sovereignty and our stewardship under Him, do hereby enter into this Christian Covenant of Partnership to govern how we will conduct ourselves toward one another, toward our work, and before God. We desire that our business be ordered not only by the laws of the state but by the law of Christ as taught in Scripture and understood in the Reformed confessions (that God owns all things, that Christians are stewards in service to one another and to our neighbor, and that we must avoid the love of money and practice justice, truth, and charity).

Accordingly, and in the fear of the Lord, we covenant and agree as follows. This Covenant shall be incorporated into the formal operating agreement of [Company Name], LLC and shall be binding upon each partner in conscience and among the partners as a rule of order and discipline.

1. Stewardship of Reserve Cash — No Interest-Bearing Accounts
1.1 Definition. “Reserve cash” means the company cash set aside for payroll, bonded obligations, emergency repairs, and ordinary operating contingencies, to be set at a level the partners approve from time to time (initially three months’ average payroll and operating costs).
1.2 Holding Requirement. No partner shall deposit, invest, lend, or otherwise place reserve cash in any interest-bearing bank account, savings account, certificate of deposit, bond, mutual fund, or other investment vehicle intended to produce interest, dividends, or return. The reserve shall be held as plain cash (i.e., negotiable currency) or, by unanimous agreement, as non-interest-bearing media expressly permitted by the partners.
1.3 Safekeeping. Reserve cash shall be kept securely in the company’s designated safe(s) at the principal place of business, in a bank safe deposit box that pays no interest (if unanimously approved), or in such other physical custody as the partners unanimously approve. Access to reserve cash shall require the signatures or presence of at least two partners or the delegated managers as the partners shall approve in writing.
1.4 Rationale. We bind ourselves to this practice because we will not trust in uncertain riches or the worldly accumulation of interest as our hope, but in God’s providence and faithful stewardship of what He entrusts to us.

2. Bringing Opportunistic Purchases and Talent Acquisitions Together
2.1 Duty to Present. When a partner becomes aware of an opportunity to acquire a competitor’s client list, to hire a competitor’s key crews, to purchase assets from a competitor or former partner in distress, or any materially similar opportunistic business advantage within our trade area, that partner shall promptly present the opportunity in writing to the partners.
2.2 First Offer to the Partnership. The partnership shall have the right of first consideration and, unless the partners unanimously decline, shall have priority to pursue the opportunity together in a manner agreed by the partners. The presenting partner shall not unilaterally take the opportunity for personal advantage without first exhausting the partnership’s consideration and receiving the unanimous consent of the other partners.
2.3 Procedure for Action. The partners shall meet or otherwise decide within five (5) business days (unless extended by common consent) whether to pursue the opportunity. If the partnership elects to proceed, the partners shall determine the terms of participation, financing, and management by unanimous agreement or by such vote as the partners agree in the operating agreement.
2.4 Purpose. We adopt this rule as shrewd stewardship and to prefer that fruitful work and opportunities remain in the hands of fellow believers where possible and appropriate.

3. Honest Books and Exact Rendering to Contractors and Suppliers
3.1 Books and Records. Each partner shall keep and maintain honest, accurate, and complete company books and records in accordance with accepted accounting principles and the company’s bookkeeping policies. All partners shall have access, on reasonable notice, to inspect the books, records, invoices, payroll records, and contracts.
3.2 Rendering Exactly What Is Contracted. The company shall render to every subcontractor, supplier, and vendor exactly what our written contract with them requires. We shall not withhold agreed compensation, misrepresent terms, or adjust deliverables to avoid payment. Any change to agreed work shall be by written amendment and mutual consent.
3.3 Remedy for Breach. If a partner is credibly alleged to have falsified records or failed to render what is contractually owed, the partners shall promptly convene to investigate. If misconduct is found, the partner responsible shall make full restitution and be subject to discipline up to removal or buyout as provided in this Covenant.

4. Partner Compensation Cap and Test of Heart
4.1 Compensation Cap. No partner shall draw a salary from the company that is higher than the wage paid to the company’s lowest-paid full-time field crew member, except as provided in this section.
4.2 Procedure to Draw More. A partner desiring to draw a higher salary must (a) notify the other partners in writing of the requested increase and the reasons therefor; (b) first live on the current lowest-paid full-time field crew wage for a continuous period of thirty (30) days, providing verifiable evidence of such living (bank statements, receipts, and a signed attestation); and (c) present himself to the partners for candid questioning about motive and need.
4.3 Approval. Only after the foregoing trial of heart and with the written agreement of at least three of the four partners (or such greater majority as the operating agreement may require) may the partner be permitted to draw a higher salary. Approval shall not be unreasonably withheld if the need is genuine and the partner has shown humility in the foregoing test.
4.4 Spirit of the Rule. This provision is adopted to guard us from covetousness and to cultivate humility, mutual solidarity with laborers, and accountability before God and one another.

5. Prior Distribution to Gospel Work
5.1 Fixed Share. Before any partner draws distributions of profit, the company shall set aside and distribute to gospel and kingdom work a fixed share of net profits in each accounting period. The initial fixed share shall be ten percent (10%) of net profit, unless the partners unanimously agree to a different percentage, in which case that agreed percentage shall be substituted and recorded in an amendment to this Covenant.
5.2 Recipients. The recipients of these funds shall be gospel ministries, church-based missions, or charities that are orthodox in doctrine and agreed upon by the partners. The partners shall review the list of recipients annually and may make adjustments by majority consent, provided recipients remain consonant with gospel work.
5.3 Timing and Accounting. The company shall distribute the fixed share within thirty (30) days after the close of each quarterly accounting period, and the distribution shall be recorded in the company books and publicly reported to the partners.

6. No Defamation or Disparagement of Competitors or Former Partners
6.1 Prohibition. No partner shall badmouth, slander, defame, or disparage in word or in writing any competitor or any former partner for the purpose of winning business or undermining that person’s reputation. This prohibition includes insinuations, dishonest comparisons, and public campaigns of denigration.
6.2 Discipline for Violation. If a partner is credibly shown to have violated Section 6.1, the partners shall require the offending partner to (a) issue a full, public retraction and apology, meeting the reasonable terms set by the injured party and the partners; (b) make restitution for verifiable financial harm caused; and (c) submit to mediation by a panel of three Christian elders mutually agreed upon by the partners (see Section 8). Repeated or egregious breaches may result in suspension of management rights or involuntary sale of the partner’s interest as provided in Section 9.

7. Amendment and Review
7.1 Amendment. No provision of this Covenant may be amended except by unanimous written consent of all partners and by a recorded amendment attached to the company operating agreement. Because this is a covenant before God, the partners commit to prayerful deliberation before any amendment.
7.2 Annual Review. The partners shall review this Covenant annually in light of experience, Scripture, and counsel from church leadership and may mutually agree to clarifying provisions consistent with the spirit of this Covenant.

8. Dispute Resolution and Ecclesiastical Counsel
8.1 Matthew 18 Process. In any controversy among partners arising under or about this Covenant, the partners shall first pursue the Matthew 18 pastoral process: private admonition, then one or two witnesses, then the church, seeking repentance and reconciliation.
8.2 Mediation and Binding Christian Arbitration. If the parties remain at issue after the Matthew 18 steps, they shall submit the matter to mediation before a panel of three mature Christian elders or pastors appointed by the church or otherwise mutually agreed upon. If mediation fails, the partners agree to binding Christian arbitration before an agreed Christian arbitration service or three Christian arbitrators selected by mutual agreement. The arbitrators shall apply biblical teaching and the terms of this Covenant; their decision shall be final among the partners.
8.3 Civil Remedies. This Covenant is intended to be a binding agreement among partners; the partners do not waive their right to seek civil remedies if required to enforce this Covenant, but they covenant to pursue the above Christian processes first, in good faith.

9. Remedies, Discipline, and Buyout for Serious Breach
9.1 Discipline. For serious breaches of this Covenant (including but not limited to dishonest bookkeeping, willful failure to render contractual obligations, repeated disparagement, or repeated disregard of the reserve-cash rule), the partners may impose discipline up to and including suspension of management authority, restitution, and removal from management, subject to the dispute resolution procedures above.
9.2 Buyout. For removal from partnership or voluntary sale under this Covenant, an involuntary buyout price shall be determined by the company’s most recent financial statements and, if disputed, by an independent appraiser agreed upon by the non-selling partners. In the case of discipline for breach, the partners may apply a penalty to the buyout price (for example, a reduction not to exceed twenty-five percent (25%) of the appraised value), the amount and terms to be determined by the arbitrators if necessary. A portion of any penalty applied for disciplinary buyout shall be distributed to the gospel fund in Section 5.
9.3 Restoration. If a disciplined partner repents and is restored per the Matthew 18 and mediation process, the partners shall seek to restore rights and relationship as Scripture and Christian charity require.

10. Conscience, Oath, and Witness
10.1 Binding Before God. We enter this Covenant mindful that we are accountable to God for our stewardship, words, and actions. We therefore bind ourselves by oath before God to keep these commitments in conscience.
10.2 Witness. We invite the elders/pastor of [church name] (or a mutually agreed Christian elder) to witness our signatures and to stand ready to advise, mediate, and admonish us according to Scripture.

Sacred Arts Policy
(For adoption by the Session of [Church Name], subject to the Westminster Confession and the Larger and Shorter Catechisms)

Preamble
We rejoice that our God is supremely knowable in Christ and that the Word (written and incarnate) governs the church’s life. This congregation is committed to worship and ministry under the rule of Scripture as interpreted by the Westminster Standards. The Scriptures’ second commandment and the Westminster Larger and Shorter Catechisms warn against making and using images as objects of religious worship or veneration. At the same time, the Standards do not require a needless abolition of all visual or representational art in every non-religious use. This policy therefore binds our practice in a way that is faithful to the Confession and Catechisms: firm against idolatry, charitable and pastoral in prudence, and practical in governance.

Purpose
- To cherish and protect the majesty of God and the centrality of Christ and the Word in our gathered worship.
- To prevent any use of visual material that would encourage photographic/venerative or liturgical reliance upon images as an object or means of grace.
- To provide clear, pastoral, and consistent guidelines for donors, ministries, leaders, and artists who seek to serve the congregation.

General Principle
- The making or use of images as objects of worship or religious veneration is forbidden in our corporate life. Visual elements that are intentionally presented to be an object, focus, or means of grace in worship are not permitted.
- Visual materials used for lawful ends — instruction, decoration, historical record, pastoral care, or congregational information — are permitted when they are plainly subordinate to the preached Word and the sacraments, do not lead to the worship or veneration of the image itself, and have Session approval.

Policy (binding rules and specific rulings)

1) Donated realistic painted portrait of Jesus hung over the communion table
Ruling: Not permitted.
Reason: Placing a large realistic portrait of our Lord as the focal image above the communion table would present a likeness as a focus for worship and prayer in a sacramental context. That use risks turning a depiction into an object of religious focus or veneration, contrary to the Confession and Catechisms’ instruction about the second commandment. The communion table must not be adorned in a way that substitutes a pictorial focus for Christ’s Word and the sacraments themselves.
Pastoral alternative offered to donor: We will gratefully receive the donor’s generosity redirected to (a) commissioning non-figurative art for the fellowship hall or education wing, (b) a donation to the church’s benevolent fund in the donor’s name, (c) a modest, non-figurative memorial in a non-liturgical space, or (d) funding for educational materials about the person and work of Christ to be used in teaching settings. The Session will work with the donor to find a suitable alternative. If the donor prefers a depiction for private devotion, they may be directed to place it in a private home or in a non-worship, clearly interpretive display in a non-liturgical area with explanatory signage and Session approval.

2) Proposal to ban ALL visual art in the building on the ground that the second commandment forbids any likeness
Ruling: Not adopted; rejected.
Reason: The Westminster Standards condemn images used for religious worship and veneration. They do not command that all likenesses in all contexts be removed from every building. A blanket ban on all visual art (architectural ornament, program photos, children’s books, banners, etc.) is an unnecessary and doctrinally unsupported severity that would hinder lawful teaching, catechesis, hospitality, and the ordinary uses of print and picture in life and ministry. Such a ban is therefore not imposed.
Qualification: Visual items that are presented, hung, or used in corporate worship in a way that makes them a focus of worship or a “means of grace” are prohibited. All visual uses (including any new commissions, banners, architectural ornament installed in worship spaces, permanent fixtures, and donated materials intended for public display) require Session approval, to be judged by these principles.

3) Children’s illustrated Bible storybooks and flannelgraph with simple drawn figures (including drawings of Jesus and the disciples) used to teach five-year-olds
Ruling: Permitted, with caution and controls.
Reason: The Westminster Standards allow lawful uses of images for instruction. Pictures that aid children’s biblical understanding are acceptable provided they are used and explained in ways that avoid idolatry.
Requirements:
- All children’s visual teaching materials used in children’s ministry must be approved by the Director of Children’s Ministry and registered with the Arts Ministry lead; materials used in a public or common area must be approved by the Session on recommendation of the Education Committee.
- Leaders must teach children that pictures are representational and not literal portraits of Jesus’ actual face and that such pictures are not objects of worship.
- Avoid highly realistic or devotional portraits of Christ that are displayed in worship spaces; keep these materials in classrooms and teaching contexts, not on the chancel or the communion table.
- Annual review: The Session will periodically review children’s visual curricula for theological and pastoral appropriateness.

4) Projected abstract non-figurative imagery behind congregational singing (light, color, moving texture; no depiction of persons of the Godhead)
Ruling: Permitted only by Session approval and under strict limitations.
Reason: Non-figurative visual accompaniment that does not depict God, Christ, or the persons of the Trinity may be used as an environment aid provided it is clearly subordinate to Word and sacrament and cannot be construed as an object of devotion or a means of grace.
Requirements:
- Any projected imagery used in the sanctuary in the gathered worship service must be approved in advance by the Session (or a Session-appointed subcommittee of elders) with recommendation from the Worship Committee.
- Such imagery must be non-figurative, not representational of any person of the Godhead or of saints, and must not include symbols that would encourage a liturgical veneration (e.g., icons, portraits, or quasi-liturgical symbols presented as efficacious).
- The worship leader and Session reserve the right to require the imagery be turned off or altered on pastoral or doctrinal grounds at any time.
- Projected imagery must never be presented, explained, or promoted as a “means of grace” or necessary for worship; it must be optional and subordinate.

5) Framed printed Scripture text and the church’s historic confession in the entryway
Ruling: Encouraged and permitted.
Reason: Displaying Scripture and our confession as texts for reading, instruction, and to declare the doctrinal identity of the congregation is consistent with the Westminster Standards and our commitment to the Word. Textual display does not constitute a forbidden image or object of worship.
Requirements:
- Such texts should be presented in a way that invites reading and instruction (with citation and context) and not as an object of veneration.
- If donors fund framing or placement, the Session will acknowledge the gift and ensure placement is consistent with this policy.

6) Requirement that any visual element used in the gathered service be approved by Session and never presented as a means of grace
Ruling: Affirmed and made binding.
Reason: The Session, as the ruling body responsible for worship (per our Presbyterian polity), will determine what is suitable for corporate worship. No visual element may be presented as conveying grace, sacramental efficacy, or as an instrument of worship apart from or in place of Word and sacrament.
Process and enforcement:
- All proposed visual elements for public worship (permanent or temporary, projected or physical) must be submitted in writing to the Worship Committee at least 30 days prior to intended use. The Worship Committee will make a recommendation to the Session. Emergency exceptions may be considered by the Session but must be reported and regularized.
- The Session retains the authority to remove any visual element introduced without approval or found to be inconsistent with this policy.
- The Session will provide an appeals process (to itself) for donors or ministry leaders who wish reconsideration; final arbitration belongs to the Session.

Additional provisions
- Donor gifts: Gifts of art will be accepted only with Session approval and an agreed placement and use plan reflecting this policy. No gift may require the church to use or display an image in contravention of this policy.
- Signage and explanation: Where helpful, especially in educational displays or in spaces where images are used for teaching, the church will include brief explanatory signage making our commitment clear: that images are pedagogical or decorative and not objects of worship.
- Teaching: The Session expects regular catechetical instruction for the congregation (adult and children’s classes) about the second commandment and the church’s practice with images so that our people understand the theological convictions shaping this policy.
- Review: The Session will review this policy at least every three years or sooner if pastoral need or significant controversy arises.

Pastoral tone
We wish to steward beauty and the arts in ways that honor God, love our neighbor, teach the faithful, and avoid scandal or temptation to idolatry. This policy is meant both to protect the church from idolatrous uses of images and to enable faithful, cautious, and creative work in the visual arts for instruction, hospitality, and the glory of God. The Session will oversee faithful application and will make every effort to work pastorally with donors, artists, and ministry leaders.
