The Confession teaches that public worship must be ordered according to the Word of God (the “regulative principle”), and that church government and discipline must be carried out according to Scripture (see the Confession’s teaching on religious worship and on church censures). For that reason I will not produce wording that (a) declares a particular unscriptural “activation” as the appointed, necessary channel of renewing grace; (b) requires physical falling or labels a conscientious person “resisting the flow”; or (c) forces monthly public confessions of private jealousies. Those provisions would be contrary to the Confession’s principles and to pastoral care as set out in Scripture (e.g., Matthew 18) and would risk coercion rather than Christian conscience and repentance.

Below is a warm but binding Worship Renewal Covenant that keeps the constructive elements you requested (start time, printed order and length, approved psalter-and-hymn singing, a regular ministry block, and a monthly members’ meeting for accountability), while aligning with the Westminster Standards’ requirements for lawful worship and lawful church discipline. WORSHIP RENEWAL COVENANT
Preamble
We, the members of [Church Name], professing our faith in the Lord Jesus Christ and subscribing to the Westminster Standards, covenant together to seek the revival and renewal of our corporate worship for God’s glory and the building up of his people. Recognizing that the Lord calls us to worship in truth and order, and that he ordinarily distributes renewing grace by means of Word and sacrament, we commit ourselves to the following practices and the session’s faithful oversight.

1. Time, Order, and Length
- We covenant to assemble for corporate worship each Lord’s Day beginning at 10:00 a.m. sharp.
- Services will follow the printed order of worship distributed in advance and will normally run about ninety (90) minutes.
- Members covenant to be present in the sanctuary at the appointed hour so that worship may proceed in orderly fashion. Repeated, unrepentant absence or disruptive lateness will be addressed by the session as a pastoral and disciplinary concern.

2. Ministry Block (designated “Ministry Time”)
- Each service will include a designated ministry block in which the leaders, under the supervision of the session, bring Scripture, prayer, pastoral proclamation, instruction, and edifying words to the congregation.
- The covenant affirms that God normally bestows sanctifying and renewing grace through the proclamation of the Word, the sacraments, and prayer by the Spirit; the ministry block is intended as an orderly, God-ordained occasion for pastoral edification and mutual upbuilding, not as a new or extra channel that replaces the Word or sacraments.
- All pastoral words given in the ministry block will be biblically tested and accountable to the session. The session will instruct the congregation in the nature, purpose, and limits of this ministry time.

3. Physical Contact and Voluntary Reception
- On rare pastoral occasions an elder or pastor may lay hands on a person in prayer (for blessing, prayer, or pastoral care), but no one shall be required to react physically in any particular way.
- Members are not compelled to fall backward, cry out, or otherwise exhibit involuntary physical responses. No member who remains standing or otherwise does not display an expected physical reaction will be labeled or recorded as “resisting the flow.”
- Any member who is distressed by pastoral practice or by the behavior of others during worship is encouraged to bring the concern first to an elder or to the session for confidential pastoral care and instruction.

4. Singing and Musical Worship
- All sung praise in public worship shall be drawn from the church’s approved psalter and hymn list. Arrangements for music shall aim to support the Word and foster congregational participation in accordance with the session’s guidance.

5. Monthly Members’ Meeting and Accountability
- A monthly members’ meeting will be held for prayer, instruction, mutual edification, and the exercise of biblical accountability under the session’s oversight.
- Members covenant to pursue Matthew 18 reconciliation (private approach, then with witnesses, then before the church) when personal grievances or jealousies arise. If a member feels personal jealousy or envy that affects the congregation, they are to seek the Lord’s grace and the guidance of the elders; the session will teach, exhort, and offer pastoral paths to confession, repentance, and restoration.
- The meeting is not a place for mandatory public confession of private emotions; however, when a sin is public or has harmed others, the session will require public repentance as Scripture and the Westminster Standards direct. Matters of private conscience may be handled privately by the elders.

6. Oversight, Enforcement, and Discipline
- This covenant is binding under the authority of the session. The session shall provide teaching on the covenant’s meaning, receive appeals, and apply correction when members persist in willful, unrepentant breaches.
- Discipline will be administered in mercy and truth, following Scripture and the practice of the Westminster Standards: admonition, admonition with rebuke, withholding of the Lord’s Supper where appropriate, and, as a last resort, exclusion from membership and office (church censure), always with a view to repentance and restoration.
- Members signing below acknowledge their willingness to submit to the session’s biblical discipline and to the teaching of the Word as the governing norm for our worship.

Signatures
We whose names follow do covenant before God and one another to seek the renewal of our worship under this covenant, and we submit to the session’s oversight in its faithful administration.

In the presence of the living God, who has graciously called me and sentenced me to love and obedience by Christ, I set down these duties as a covenant before Him. I make them solemn and simple so my heart may be steadfast instead of swinging between terror and defiance. I do this humbly, knowing I am bound ultimately to Christ and to the authority of Scripture and the church; these rules are for my conscience and conduct, not a claim that God receives me because of any outward rite.

- I will present this Rule to my pastor/elders and ask their counsel, and I will be willing to have these commitments examined and corrected by them in love. I will return to the Word if God, by Scripture and by faithful brethren, calls me to adjust what I have written.

A few controlling principles from the standards
- The Tenth Commandment requires “full contentment with our own condition” and forbids “all discontentment with our own estate, envying, and such like” (Shorter Catechism on the tenth commandment). Contentment is a required grace; covetousness and envy are forbidden.
- The Standards also teach the duties of marriage and the household: marriage is a God‑ordained relation for mutual help and holy living (WCF, ch. 24). Husbands and wives are to discharge their duties in love, faithfulness, and mutual care.
- Public worship and the Lord’s Day are duties Christians must not neglect (WCF, ch. 21). A Christian is obliged to family duties and to works of religion, mercy, and justice as fruits of faith.

How these apply to your wife taking a modest part‑time bookkeeping job
- It is not automatically covetous for a wife to work and have a little of her own. The Tenth Commandment forbids discontentment and inordinate desire; it does not forbid lawful, modest labor or a small degree of independence when the work is lawful and motives are right.
- The Westminster Standards expect mutual help within marriage. If her work is meant to relieve the household burden, to practice useful gifts, to contribute to the family, to give her healthy time away for personal well‑being, or to enable charity and stewardship, those are not necessarily sins and can be consistent with “contentment with our own condition.”
- On the other hand, if her work springs from envy, rebellion against your role, a deliberate desire to assert financial independence in a way that undermines marital duties, or prideful discontent with the provision God has given through you, then the Tenth Commandment’s prohibition against discontent and covetousness would be implicated.

Practical counsel about your wife
- Don’t command her to quit as your first move. Approach her with biblical love: ask about her motives, listen, pray together, seek pastoral counsel if needed, and weigh whether her labor helps or hinders your mutual duties. The Standards call for husbands and wives to act in mutual help and charity, not by unilateral domination.

How these apply to your overwork and motive to out‑earn your brother‑in‑law
- Your stated motive — to out‑earn and “beat” your brother‑in‑law because he gibes you — is classic territory for covetousness, envy, and pride. The Tenth Commandment requires contentment and forbids envying another’s estate and “all inordinate motions and affections” toward riches.
- The Standards also require Christians to keep the Lord’s Day and to attend public worship. Neglecting the corporate worship of the church and the Sabbath for the sake of selling is a serious failure of duty (WCF ch. 21). Likewise, husbands have duties to their wives and children to lead in love and to care for them (WCF ch. 24). Constant overwork to the point of family neglect violates those duties.
- Stewardship and providence are virtues — the Standards commend industry and wise management of God’s gifts — but they are not license for idolatry of earning, neglect of worship, or failure in family duties. Purposes and priorities matter.

Practical counsel about you
- Repent of the motive of rivalry and covetousness. Confess and renounce the desire to excel chiefly to satisfy pride or envy.
- Reorder your priorities to restore Sabbath and public worship, to set firm limits on late nights and days off, and to give your family adequate time and presence. The Standards require both family duties and regular public worship.
- Reassess the side hustles: are they for necessary provision, stewardship, and charity, or are they driven by envy and pride? Keep what is needed and helpful; cut or limit what undermines marriage and worship.
- Talk honestly with your wife: repent together where needed, decide mutually what roles and labors serve your family and godliness, and consider pastoral guidance and practical steps (budgeting, delegation, scheduled family times, a set day of rest).

Bottom line
- I cannot affirm your blanket commands. The Westminster Standards call you to repent of covetous motives and to honor family and worship duties. They do not automatically condemn a modest, well‑motivated part‑time job for your wife; but they do condemn your present motive and the way your work is trampling sacramental and family duties. Change your motive and your schedule; treat your wife with charity and discuss her work together, rather than ordering her to quit.

With that in view, below is a warm but binding Order of Gathering you can adopt covenantally, drafted to keep the rhythm you want while staying faithful to the teaching of the Westminster Confession and Catechisms: it makes weekly meeting a clear covenant duty, keeps corporate prayer, Scripture, charity and fellowship central, provides for prayer and anointing for the sick, and lays out church discipline — but it removes the elements that would turn anointing into a weekly sacramental rite or require public confession merely for an absence. Brief theological principles (from the Westminster Standards that guide these changes)
- Worship must be ordered by Christ’s Word (the regulative principle); the Confession limits sacraments to Baptism and the Lord’s Supper. Practices added to worship must not be presented as new sacraments or as having sacramental efficacy that Scripture does not give.
- The church must care for the sick and practice prayer and pastoral ministry; anointing with oil and laying on of hands for healing are pastoral practices of prayer, not additional sacraments.
- Church discipline is prescribed, but it must be exercised according to Scripture: private admonition first, proportionate measures, and public censure only for unrepentant or scandalous sin that harms the body.

Because of those principles:

Order of Gathering (Covenant for Households)
Preamble
We covenant before God to gather weekly as households to worship, to hear God’s Word, to exercise mutual care and discipline, and to encourage one another in the faith. We submit this Order of Gathering as a binding covenant among us. By signing this covenant a household promises to keep these practices and to submit to the brotherly oversight of the elders and the fellowship.

1. Opening (psalm or hymn; prayer)
- We open each gathering with a psalm or a biblically-sound hymn and a brief prayer of adoration, confession, and petition. Singing and prayer are essential parts of our worship.

2. Scripture reading and brief teaching
- One of the gathered reads aloud a passage of Holy Scripture and gives a brief exposition and application aimed at encouraging obedience and faith in Christ. The preaching/teaching is central and never omitted.

3. Prayer ministry for the sick (anointing with oil)
- When any among us is sick or requests prayer for healing, we will bring them forward and pray for them, laying on of hands and using anointing with oil as a sign of prayer and dependence on God.
- The oil kept for this purpose (our “healing jar”) is a practical provision for pastoral prayer; we will steward it carefully. However, we explicitly affirm that the oil is a sign used in prayer, not a sacrament, and that God’s promise of healing is received by faith in Him, not by the mechanical presence or weekly filling of a jar.
- Use of the oil and laying on of hands are to be exercised by an elder or an appointed elderly brother/sister under elder oversight; they are to be accompanied by prayer, Scripture, and pastoral counsel. Anointing will be performed when there is need, not as a compulsory weekly rite.

4. Attendance covenant and accountability
- We covenant to meet together weekly unless prevented by unavoidable reasons (serious illness, hospitalization, legitimate urgent necessity). Households must notify the elders if they must miss a gathering.
- A solitary, inadvertent missed week for a legitimate reason is not automatic public sin. If a household misses without notice or with an unjustified pattern of absence, the elders will first seek private counsel and admonition (Matthew 18:15–17). Only where an absence evidences unrepentant neglect of covenant duties, persistent rebellion, or public scandal will the matter be brought before the congregation and public confession required.
- Repeated, unrepentant neglect after private admonition can lead to progressive measures (private admonition → public admonition → suspension from participation in corporate privileges → removal from membership) in line with Scripture and church discipline as outlined in our bylaws.

5. Offering for one another’s needs
- We take up a voluntary offering to meet the needs of members and neighbors. Giving is to be free, cheerful, and according to ability, administered by the elders or appointed stewards.

6. Common meal and the Lord’s Supper
- We share a common meal of Christian fellowship in love. This meal is distinct from the Lord’s Supper.
- The Lord’s Supper will be celebrated in due order under elder oversight at a stated frequency agreed by the fellowship (monthly, quarterly, or at another agreed interval). The sacrament is to be administered only as instituted by Christ and is not to be confused with the common meal.

7. Prayer, confession, and pastoral care
- We will include time for intercessory prayer, mutual confession where appropriate, and pastoral counsel. Where private sins are confessed, pastoral confidentiality will be respected unless such sins create public scandal.

8. Stewardship of the “healing jar” and pastoral practices
- The elders are responsible to keep the anointing oil accessible and to teach rightly about its use. No household or person will treat the jar or the frequency of its use as a magical guarantee or as a condition for God’s blessing.
- The fellowship will maintain the jar as a symbol and tool of pastoral care; its being filled is a matter of stewardship, not liturgical efficacy.

9. Discipline, reconciliation, and restoration
- Discipline will aim at repentance and restoration. It will be administered privately first, then with increasing openness only as Scripture warrants. Public confession is reserved for public or scandalous sin or for the restoration process where appropriate; it is not required for every unexcused absence.

10. Commitment and signatures
- Each household that signs this covenant binds itself to these practices and to the authority of the elders in administering the order and discipline here described. To alter these terms requires the consent of the elders and a two‑thirds vote of the households.

Closing encouragement
We bind ourselves to this Order because we desire to worship God in a way ordered by Scripture, to care for one another in love, to encourage holiness, and to preserve the purity of the church. May our gatherings be marked by reverence, grace, and the power of the Word.

Contentment Covenant of [Group Name]

Preamble
We, the members of [Group Name], do hereby enter into this solemn covenant before the LORD who owns all things and cares for His people. Motivated by Scripture and the historic Reformed teaching on providence, stewardship, charity, and the duty of contentment, we bind ourselves to one another for mutual aid, plain living, spiritual growth, and the right use of money. Our covenant is voluntary, biblical, and binding upon conscience; it is designed not to shame but to form us in Christlike contentment (the opposite of covetousness), faithful generosity, and disciplined simplicity. We intend regular pastoral and mutual accountability, and we submit to brotherly correction where a member persists in breach without repentance.

Articles of the Covenant

1. Priority of Giving
- Each member covenants to give at least ten percent (10%) of gross personal income as regular support for the local church or other gospel work approved by the group.
- Gifts will be recorded monthly in the group’s shared giving sheet, with a line item for amount, recipient (church or gospel work), and date. Receipts or screenshots will be attached when practicable.
- If a member believes exigent circumstances justify temporary reduction below 10%, they will bring that need to their accountability partner and the group at the next monthly meeting for prayer and counsel.

2. Major Purchases and the Median Standard
- For purposes of guarding against status-driven consumption, we adopt the group median of member home values, car values, and typical vacation cost as an ethical benchmark.
- No member shall purchase a home, automobile, or vacation costing more than the then-current group median for that category without first bringing a clear proposal to the group and receiving the group’s approval in accordance with the process below.
- The group median will be computed annually from the values recorded in the shared asset sheet. The Treasurer (or designated member) will publish the median within two weeks of calculation.
- Approval process: the proposing member must submit (a) the proposed purchase price and financing plan, (b) a budget showing its impact on tithing and necessary household provision, and (c) their pastoral/accountability partner’s written recommendation. The group will discuss and offer counsel; approval requires a simple majority of present, participating members. If the group declines, the member will not proceed while a part of this covenant community.

3. Heart-Work Against Envy
- We covenant to cultivate gratitude and rejoice in a brother’s or sister’s prosperity rather than desire for what they have. We acknowledge the tenth commandment’s prohibition of covetousness and the call to contentment.
- Any member who becomes aware of envy in themselves regarding another member’s possessions, position, or prosperity will confess that envy to their accountability partner and publicly to the group within the following week (or sooner if requested by the accountability partner).
- Confession is to be candid, specific about the tempted desire, and include a plan for repentance and practical change agreed with the accountability partner.

4. Limits on Pursuit of Greater Wealth
- Recognizing that a chief root of discontent is the restless pursuit of more, each member covenants not to actively pursue a raise, promotion, or second income stream for the purpose of increasing lifestyle beyond what is needed for daily provision and reasonable household obligations.
- “Pursue” means actively seeking or applying for higher-paying positions, initiating side-business ventures for added personal consumption, or negotiating for compensation increases primarily to fund non-essential wants.
- Exceptions: urgent and godly reasons related to necessary provision for dependents, medical needs, catastrophic loss, or a clear call to gospel service may justify seeking additional income. In such cases the member will bring the circumstances to their accountability partner and the group before proceeding; the group will pray, advise, and grant counsel. Emergency situations after the fact must be disclosed as soon as feasible.
- Members remain committed to faithful labor, competence in their calling, and doing work to God’s glory; this Article does not permit idleness.

5. The “Enough” Journal
- Each member will keep a monthly “Enough” journal listing what they already have that meets needs and brings thankful contentment (housing, clothing, tools, furniture, leisure, digital devices, etc.), and noting where they lack what is necessary.
- The “Enough” entry shall be completed and shared with the member’s accountability partner by the 5th day of each month. The accountability partner will read, pray, and offer at least one piece of constructive counsel or encouragement within seven days.

6. Open Budgets and Monthly Meetings
- We commit to meet monthly for mutual counsel and prayer. At each meeting members will open their monthly household budgets for honest, humble review and wise counsel.
- Budgets include income, tithes/giving, fixed expenses, debt payments, savings, and discretionary spending. Members will bring a printed or shared copy to the meeting.
- Meetings will be conducted in a spirit of encouragement, sufficiency, and pastoral correction — not of shame or competitiveness. The group may propose practical adjustments and will follow up in subsequent meetings.

7. Accountability, Restoration, and Discipline
- A member who violates this covenant is expected to confess and make restitution where applicable. The accountability partner will seek immediate pastoral and group support for repentance.
- If a member refuses to repent after private appeals by the accountability partner, the matter will be brought to the monthly meeting for brotherly admonition and prayer. Continued, unrepentant breach may result in suspension from the covenant for a season, with restoration contingent on repentance.
- Records of confessions and discipline are confidential within the accountability relational circle and the monthly meeting, unless the member gives broader consent or the matter requires civil reporting (e.g., theft, fraud).

8. Amendments and Duration
- This covenant is entered freely and voluntarily and will remain in force while the member wishes to belong to [Group Name]. It may be amended only by a two-thirds vote of active members following a thirty-day notice and a period of group prayer.
- A member may depart the covenant by written notice to the group; we will meet to pray and seek restoration if the member later desires to return.

9. Signatory Declaration
I hereby, before God and these brothers and sisters, subscribe to this Contentment Covenant of [Group Name], promising to keep the duties herein faithfully to the glory of God, to love and bear with my fellow members in meekness, and to submit to the agreed processes of accountability and restoration. I acknowledge that this covenant is both spiritual and practical: spiritual in that it binds conscience before the LORD, and practical in that it binds us to honest mutual aid.

Short answer up front
- Streaming the service for shut‑ins is not forbidden by the Westminster Standards and may be a lawful, pastoral use of “circumstances” (adiaphora) so long as it does not alter the instituted elements of worship or introduce things contrary to Scripture. The Session has the authority to regulate how it is done, but an elder may not simply declare all cameras and screens “worldly” and tear them out as if that were required by our Standards.  
- A “virtual Lord’s Supper” in which people at home “self‑serve” bread and wine when the pastor speaks over a camera is not permitted by the Westminster Standards. The Lord’s Supper is a sacrament, a visible sign and seal of the covenant, appointed to be administered by Christ’s officers to the visible church; it is not a private, unauthorised, or purely mediated act.

How I reach those conclusions from the Standards
1) Governing principle: regulative principle and the distinction between substance and circumstance
- The Standards require that public worship be ordered according to Scripture and that we not invent new worship elements (the regulative principle). That controls the substance of worship (preaching the Word, prayer, singing, the sacraments, etc.).  
- But the Standards also recognize that many things about worship are “circumstances” (time, place, light, number, the particular means used to communicate) and are left to Christian prudence and the church’s judgment, provided they do not contravene Scripture or the nature of the instituted worship. These adiaphora may be altered for the edification of the church.

Application to streaming
- Cameras, screens and audio/web streaming are means of communicating the instituted elements (Scripture, preaching, prayer, singing, and so on) to members who cannot be physically present. They are, in themselves, circumstances/adaptations, not new sacraments or additions to worship. Used prudently they are lawful aids for pastoral care (visiting shut‑ins, enabling the sick/aged to hear the Word and join in worship mentally and spiritually).  
- The Session has authority to regulate how streaming is done: what is shown, how interaction is handled, whether the camera broadcasts the ordinance table during the sacrament, etc. That regulation should aim to preserve the reverence, order, and distinctions that the Standards require. An elder may urge caution, but may not unilaterally forbid a lawful use simply because he considers the device “worldly.” A blanket prohibition that removes lawful pastoral provision without biblical warrant would itself be an overreach.

Practical safeguards for streaming consistent with the Standards
- Continue streaming for shut‑ins as a legitimate pastoral means, unless the Session judges some specific, concrete problem requires restriction.  
- Limit the stream so it communicates the service (audio and/or a single camera) without creating confusion about participation. Disable live chats or interactive features that could blur the line between being present and being physically part of the gathered assembly.  
- Do not treat streaming as creating a parallel “congregation.” Make clear pastoral guidance to remote viewers about their role: they may observe, pray, be nourished spiritually by the Word, but are not to claim they are part of the gathered communion unless they are physically present or properly represented under church order.  
- If privacy or order concerns exist (e.g., showing the sacrament table), handle those by policy (e.g., camera off or focused elsewhere during distribution).

2) The Lord’s Supper: why “virtual communion” is unlawful under the Standards
- The Standards teach that sacraments are holy signs and seals instituted by Christ to be administered by his appointed officers to the visible church. The external, visible administration of the elements under the ministry of the church is essential to their character as signs and seals.  
- The Lord’s Supper is not merely a private devotion or an individual act of remembrance; it is a corporate, ministered ordinance of the church. “Self‑serving” elements at home timed to a minister’s words on a screen substitutes private action for public administration and breaks the connection between the sacrament as administered by the church’s officers and the visible fellowship of the communicants. Because it changes the nature of the sacrament’s external sign and seal, it is not a legitimate administration of the Lord’s Supper under the Standards.
- There is a proper way, under church order, to care for those who cannot be present (see next section). But broadcasting the pastor’s words over a camera and instructing people to eat what they have on hand is not an administration of the sacrament as the Standards require.

Pastoral and ecclesiastical alternatives consistent with the Standards
- The Session and pastor may arrange for the Lord’s Supper to be taken to shut‑ins in a way consistent with the Standards: ministers or elders may make pastoral visits and administer the sacrament to housebound members according to church order (these are private administrations of the sacrament to those unable to attend, carried out by officers of the church). This preserves ministerial administration and visible application of the elements. (This is very different from telling people over the internet to eat their own bread simultaneously.)  
- If home visitation and home communion by an officer is impractical, the Session should create a policy for how those who cannot attend are to be ministered to (e.g., visitation communions at another time, spiritual communion by prayer and meditation on Scripture until a proper administration can occur).  
- Streaming the service is permissible and can continue, but the sacrament must not be administered virtually. The minister should not instruct remote viewers to partake at home as if that were the Lord’s Supper.

What the Session should do now (procedural/disciplinary guidance)
- The Session should meet, apply the Standards, and make a corporate ruling: (a) whether and on what terms the service will be streamed; (b) that the Lord’s Supper will not be administered virtually; and (c) what provisions will be made for shut‑ins to receive the sacrament legitimately (home visits, scheduled private communions, or other appropriate pastoral care).  
- If the elder insists on an absolute ban on camera/screen devices contrary to the Session’s decision, the Session should correct him by reason and, if necessary, follow the church’s discipline in love (the Standards assign care and correction to the Session). If the pastor insists on proceeding with virtual communion contrary to the Session’s ruling and the Standards, the Session must bar him from doing so and exercise its oversight (including admonition and, if obstinacy continues, further church discipline). The minister is not free to change the mode of any sacrament in opposition to the church’s rule and the Standards.

Concrete technical guidance for you (as tech)
- Continue to run the stream subject to Session approval and the safeguards above.  
- Ensure camera angles/content policies (e.g., do not show the distribution of the elements, or go off-air during the sacrament if the Session prefers that). If the Session forbids streaming the sacrament, stop the stream for that portion.  
- Do not assist or enable any “virtual communion” practice; if asked to set up anything that would appear to endorse or facilitate it (e.g., a “join in now” slide, clickable elements, or special broadcasts timed for self‑serving), decline and refer the matter to the Session.  
- Keep documentation of Session policy in writing and follow it.

Bottom line
- Streaming for shut‑ins is a lawful pastoral accommodation under the Standards when regulated by the Session; tearing out cameras on the ground that they are inherently “worldly” would be an unwarranted forbidding of a lawful circumstantial means.  
- Administering the Lord’s Supper by telling remote people to take their own elements at home at the pastor’s prompt is not a lawful administration of the sacrament under the Westminster Standards. The Session must prohibit that and provide pastoral alternatives consistent with our confessional order.

If you want, I can draft (1) a short Session policy you can present tomorrow authorizing streaming with specific safeguards, and (2) suggested wording the Session can use to instruct the congregation (and the pastor) about the church’s position on virtual communion and on pastoral options for shut‑ins.

House Rule of Life — Covenant of the [House Name]
Preamble
We, the members of this discipleship house, covenant together before God and one another to live under the Lordship of Jesus Christ, to pursue holiness, mutual edification, and faithful stewardship of all the resources the Lord entrusts to us. In keeping with Scripture and the biblical principles reflected in the Reformed standard that guides our life together, we acknowledge that Christians are called to contentment, to flee covetousness, and to submit to godly authority and mutual accountability for the sake of growth in Christ. Therefore, as a voluntary and solemn commitment, each resident signs this Rule of Life and agrees to be bound by its requirements and the accountability processes it prescribes.

Section I — Our Commitments
1. Our central rhythms
  a. Attendance. Every resident commits to regular participation in the house’s worship and discipleship gatherings: Sunday worship/gathering and midweek (Wednesday) discipleship meeting. Attendance is required unless excused by leaders for legitimate reasons (illness, unavoidable work obligations, or other emergencies).
  b. Mutual care. We will pray for and care for one another, speak the truth in love, and practice confession and restoration when sin is present.

2. Stewardship, contentment, and financial limits
  a. Monthly cap on earning, saving, and spending. Each resident accepts a monthly cap on personal income, saving, and discretionary spending set by the house leaders in consultation with the household. The cap is intended to cultivate contentment and to limit the pursuit of more that feeds covetousness. The leaders will announce the cap and any changes at least one month before they take effect.
  b. Seeking increases, side income, or raises. Any effort to increase earnings (asking for a raise, taking a side job, or engaging in new income-generating ventures) requires prior written approval from the house leaders. This policy is not to control legitimate vocation but to exercise caution against ambition that fosters covetousness and disrupts our discipleship priorities.
  c. Shared transparency. Every resident’s relevant household finances (income within the scope of the cap, contributions to the common fund, and agreed household obligations) will be recorded on the house’s shared budget spreadsheet, which is visible to all house members.

3. Purchases and community discernment
  a. Purchases over $40. Any personal or household purchase over $40 must be posted to the house communication channel within 24 hours prior to purchase when reasonably possible. The house has up to 48 hours to weigh in. This practice is designed to “kill covetousness in community” by inviting counsel and mutual accountability. In case of genuine urgency, a leader may authorize an exception in advance.
  b. Shared purchases. Items intended for common use or that materially affect shared finances must be approved in advance according to the decision process described in Section III.

4. Chores and common life
  a. Chore contribution. All residents will participate faithfully in shared chores according to a schedule maintained by house leadership. Regular non-participation after admonition and correction will be treated as a breach of covenant.
  b. Common meal fund. All residents contribute to the house common meal fund at an amount set monthly by the leaders and agreed upon in the house meeting. The fund covers communal groceries and shared meals.

5. Geographic stability and departure
  a. Acceptance of outside offers. A resident may not accept a job offer that requires relocating to another city without a written release from the house leaders. This rule protects the life and witness of our household and seeks to prevent discontentment disguised as opportunity.
  b. Release process. To request release, a resident submits a written request stating the offer, its terms, and reasons. Leaders will meet with the resident within seven days, pray, and give a decision within 14 days. Release may be granted with reasonable terms for transition; if refused, the resident may either remain under covenant or resign the covenant voluntarily by giving the agreed notice (see Section III). If a resident leaves without following this process, it will be deemed a breach of covenant and will invoke the disciplinary steps below.

Section II — Authority, review, and amendment
1. Leadership role. House leaders are entrusted to administer these rules, to care pastorally for residents, to call residents to repentance, and to apply correction in love. Leaders do not seek to dominate but to shepherd.
2. Setting and adjusting the cap and funds. The leaders set the monthly income/spending cap and the common meal contribution amount, reviewing them at least quarterly in consultation with residents and with sensitivity to fairness and necessity.
3. Amendments. Material changes to this Rule of Life will be proposed to the house, discussed openly, and approved by house leaders. Significant changes will take effect only after a one-month notice.

Section III — Decision processes, exceptions, and accountability
1. Requesting exceptions. A resident may request a temporary or permanent exception to any rule by submitting a written rationale to the leaders. Leaders will prayerfully consider and respond within 14 days.
2. Discipline for breach. If a resident breaks any covenantal commitment:
  a. First step — private admonition. A leader meets with the resident to call to repentance and set clear steps to restore obedience.
  b. Second step — house accountability. If unrepentant or if the breach recurs, the matter is brought before the leaders and, if appropriate, the whole house for accountability and restoration.
  c. Third step — probation. Continued failure after admonition may result in a period of probation with specific conditions (e.g., restricted privileges, increased accountability meetings).
  d. Final step — dismissal from the house. If the resident remains unrepentant or flagrantly violates the covenant in a way that harms the household, leaders may terminate residency. Termination will include a reasonable schedule for moving out and settlement of any shared financial obligations. A resident who departs without release forfeits certain house privileges and may be required to make restitution as determined by leaders.
3. Appeal. A resident may appeal a leaders’ decision by requesting a review hearing where at least two other mature Christians outside the leadership, agreed upon by both resident and leaders, will examine the case and recommend action.

Section IV — Practical provisions
1. Moving out and deposits. The covenant includes an agreed move-out notice period (normally 30 days), and any security deposit or shared financial responsibilities will be handled per the house’s financial policy.
2. Privacy and transparency. While financial transparency is required as above for house matters, leaders covenant to protect confidential pastoral information, sharing only what is necessary for accountability.
3. Term limits and renewal. Residency in this discipleship house is for a term (commonly 6–12 months), renewable by mutual agreement. Renewal requires a review meeting with leaders.

Closing covenant
We enter this Rule of Life willingly and solemnly before God. We understand that this is not merely a set of rules but a covenantal way of life intended to shape hearts toward Christlike contentment, brotherly/sisterly love, and holy obedience. We submit to these practices under Christ, seeking His grace and the sanctifying work of the Holy Spirit.

Short answer up front
- Feature A (reading planner, reminders, streaks, sermon audio): lawful. It is a permissible use of indifferent means (adiaphora) to promote Scripture reading and hearing the Word, provided elders set prudent guardrails so the features are not sinful or scandalous. An elder may not forbid every such tool as if it were intrinsically corrupting.
- Feature B (AI “Daily Word” written in God’s voice to each user): unlawful as proposed. It purports to give new revelation “from the Lord” and so conflicts with the Confession’s teaching that Scripture alone is the rule for faith and that God’s people must not invent or receive new revelations or appeals to private inspiration.

Reasoning from the Westminster Standards

1) The governing principles
- The Holy Scripture is the sole, sufficient, authoritative rule of faith and life. The church must not add to God’s revelation or treat inventions of men as divine (WCF, chapter on Holy Scripture; see also the Regulative Principle in the chapter on religious worship).  
- Christian liberty: believers may lawfully use things indifferent (adiaphora) that Scripture neither commands nor forbids, so long as they are used without sin, do not set aside a divine command, and do not cause a weaker brother to stumble (WCF, chapter on Christian Liberty).  
- Worship and God’s ordinances are to be performed according to God’s revealed appointment; we must not invent new modes, rites, or revelations and present them as worship or divine communication (WCF, chapter on Religious Worship and the Sabbath Day).

2) Application to Feature A
- The content of Feature A — Scripture reading plans, reminders, streak tracking, and a library of the church’s sermons — plainly serves the ends the Standards commend: hearing, reading, and meditating on God’s Word and the sanctifying use of means. These are lawful “expedients” to promote piety.
- The Confession’s doctrine of Christian liberty supports using indifferent means so long as they are not sinful in themselves and are used prudently and charitably. A blanket prohibition of all reading tools would be an unlawful restraint of lawful liberty.
- Practical caveats consistent with the Standards: the elders should exercise oversight to prevent abuse. Examples of reasonable guardrails:
  - Make streaks, badges, leaderboards, and other gamified social-competition features optional and not front-and-center; avoid encouraging pride, superstition, or legalism. (Using them as aids is different from treating them as spiritual tests.)
  - Reminders should be configurable and pastoral in tone; they must not be presented as a sacramental or obligatory sign of God’s favor.
  - Sermon audio must be doctrinally faithful, clearly attributed, and not mixed with anything that might claim special revelation.
  - Provide user guidance that these tools are aids to devotion, not substitutes for public worship, sacraments, pastoral oversight, or Scripture itself.
- Conclusion on A: permit, with prudential controls. An elder who would forbid all such tools is going beyond the Standards.

3) Application to Feature B
- The app feature as described produces, each morning, a first-person “word from the Lord” particularized to the user. That presents human/computer-generated text as divine speech. The Standards reject adding new revelation and receiving private inspirations as authoritative: Scripture alone is the rule and measure. The church must not present invented messages as if they come from God.
- Such a feature risks false prophecy, misleading consciences, and undermining the sufficiency and finality of Scripture and the ordinary means Christ has appointed (preaching, sacraments, prayer, Scripture). That conflicts with the Confession’s teaching and the Regulative Principle.
- Therefore the specific design — AI-generated “My child, today I am calling you…” addressed as from God — is unlawful and must not be shipped.
- Pastoral alternatives consistent with our Standards:
  - Offer a daily devotional reflection written or approved by ordained pastoral staff and explicitly labeled “Pastoral Devotional” or “Daily Reflection,” not “Word from the Lord.”  
  - If you use AI to draft materials, require human pastoral editing/approval and clear disclosure that the text is a human (or AI-assisted) devotional reflection, not direct revelation.
  - Provide Scripture-centered “prompts” or Bible verses keyed to a user’s entries (e.g., “Scripture for you today: Psalm 23”), but never present those as spoken by God to the person in the first person.
  - Acknowledge the limits of technology and emphasize submission to Scripture, preaching, and pastoral counsel.

Practical recommendation for the elders and product team
- Approve Feature A with the guardrails above; document pastoral oversight and user guidance. Make gamification optional and modest. Keep sermon archive doctrinally vetted.
- Reject Feature B in its present, first-person, divine-voice form. Propose as a replacement a Scripture-based daily devotional (pastorally written or pastor-reviewed) and/or an AI-assisted “suggested Scripture and reflection” clearly labeled as such and not presented as a direct word from God.
- Encourage the elders to frame their disagreements under the Standards: one side treating adiaphora as illicit is overstrict; the other side treating technological novelty as equivalent to God’s Word is dangerously lax. The Confession calls for liberty rightly limited by Scripture, the Regulative Principle, and pastoral charity.

If you’d like, I can draft suggested wording for app copy, settings, and the elders’ resolution that implements these guardrails in concrete product terms.

Short answer — sorted by the Westminster Standards:

- (i) Stage lighting, fog machine, in‑ear click tracks: broadly permissible as “things indifferent” (tools/circumstances) so long as they are used to promote decent, orderly, Scripturally‑founded worship and not to replace or pretend to be an element of worship instituted by Scripture. They are not in themselves forbidden, but their use must be governed by the regulative principle and by pastoral prudence.

- (ii) Structuring the set to manufacture an emotional “wave” and attributing goosebumps or the produced feeling as the Spirit’s presence: not permissible. The Standards require that worship be conducted according to God’s revealed will, not the devices of men; presenting manufactured emotional states as the Spirit’s work is a confusion of human artifice with divine action and falls under the kind of “will‑worship” and error the Confession warns against.

- (iii) Improvised “impressions” delivered as direct messages from the Lord to particular people: not permissible as public authoritative revelation. The Confession affirms the sufficiency of Scripture and forbids adding to the rule of faith by new revelations; public claims of specific divine messages in ordinary worship must be tested and regulated by the eldership and may not be presented as normative or binding.

Why (briefly, from the Standards)
- The controlling principle is the Regulative Principle of Worship in the Westminster Confession: the acceptable way of worshipping God is prescribed by His Word and must not be fashioned by the imaginations and devices of men. (WCF, chap. 21, esp. the paragraphs teaching that worship must be according to God’s revealed will.)
- The Confession also teaches that the whole counsel of God necessary for faith and life is contained in Scripture and that nothing is to be added by new revelations or private impressions (WCF chap. 1 statements about Scripture’s sufficiency and against new revelations).

Practical pastoral guidance for the elders and worship team
1. Test everything by the Word. Ask: does this practice point people to Christ and the means of grace (Word, sacraments, prayer, praise) and preserve decency and order? If yes, it may be allowed with limits; if it supplants or obscures God’s appointed means, remove it.
2. Adopt clear, written worship practices:
   - Allow technical aids (monitors, in‑ears, lighting for visibility, sound) when they serve clarity, order, and the congregational good. Require they not be used primarily to manipulate feelings or distract from preaching and sacraments.
   - Prohibit theatrical manipulations designed to manufacture spiritual experiences (e.g., deliberate fog/sound/lighting shifts timed to force an emotional climax and then declared to be the Spirit).
   - Prohibit the giving of spontaneous “messages from the Lord” in corporate worship. If team members report subjective impressions they think may be from the Lord, require they bring them to the elders privately for testing against Scripture before anything is announced publicly.
3. Re‑teach the congregation and team about how the Spirit works according to Scripture — He works through the Word and sacraments, produces fruit and obedience, and must be tested by Scripture (the Standards press this point).
4. If the worship leader persists in presenting manipulated experiences or untested impressions as divine, the elders must act: counsel, correction, and if necessary removal from leadership until repentance and restoration occur, following the church’s oversight under the Confession’s teaching about church government and discipline.

If you want, I can draft (a) a short policy statement for your session about use of technology and prohibition of claimed impressions in worship, and (b) a brief set of questions the elders can use to evaluate any worship practice by the Standards.

Short answer up front
- Your wanting a higher-paying, less-abusive job is not automatically the sin of covetousness. It can be a lawful, even godly, desire when your motive is stewardship, health, and using your talents — not envy or an inordinate love of money. You may and should consider the new opportunity.
- Secretly copying the client list and the pricing playbook and taking them to the new employer is wrong. That is taking what belongs to another (breach of trust/property), and the Westminster Standards, following the moral law, require honest dealing, forbidding theft and deceit even when you feel wronged.

How I reach that (from the Westminster moral teaching and its logic)
1) Covetousness and lawful desire
- The Westminster Standards treat the moral law (the Ten Commandments) as binding and explain that the tenth commandment forbids inordinate and unlawful desires for another’s goods and the sinful motions of the heart that lead to wanting what is another’s to the hurt of charity and contentment. But they also affirm duties such as providence, stewardship, and sobriety of life.
- Desiring a fair wage, refusing abusive treatment, and seeking to provide for yourself and your dependents are legitimate. The Standards do not teach that Christians must never change circumstances or seek better pay; rather they call for contentment of spirit in the Christian’s heart and honest conduct in the world.
- The practical test is motive and means: Is your desire rooted primarily in greed, envy, or a restless love of money? Or is it rooted in a desire to steward God’s gifts, preserve your health and witness, and serve faithfully? The former is sinful covetousness; the latter is lawful.

2) Theft, breach of trust, and restitution
- The Westminster teaching upholds the moral law against stealing and the duty to truth, fidelity, and justice. Secretly copying proprietary client lists, pricing playbooks, or other company-confidential materials without permission is appropriation of another’s goods and a breach of confidence. It is not made right by your manager’s earlier injustice.
- The Standards (reflecting Scripture) prohibit returning wrong for wrong. Even when badly treated, Christians are to keep to honesty, not to practice deceit or theft to “level the score.” If you have been wronged, pursue redress by lawful means (documenting the abuse, talking with HR, bringing complaints, seeking restitution where appropriate), but do not commit a wrong yourself.

Practical steps you can take now
- Examine your heart. Pray and ask God to reveal whether this desire is stewardship‑minded or covetous. Confess any bitterness, envy, or covetousness and ask for grace to act rightly.
- Take the interview. There is nothing inherently sinful about exploring and accepting better lawful employment.
- Review your employment agreement and company policies (confidentiality, IP, non‑solicit clauses). What is the contract/legal ownership of the list and playbook? If you are unsure, seek legal advice before doing anything with those materials.
- Do not copy or download proprietary documents or client lists without permission. If some client relationships were built by you personally and you have private contact details you legitimately collected on your own time (and not as company property), the situation is more nuanced; still be cautious and avoid secretive appropriation.
- If you built relationships, once you have left you may contact former clients in a straightforward, lawful, and non‑deceptive way — but don’t use stolen documents or confidential trade information to solicit them.
- Seek remedy for your manager’s mistreatment through appropriate channels (HR, documented complaints), and consider whether a frank but measured conversation or formal complaint is right before leaving. But do not use the wrongs you suffered as moral cover for dishonesty.
- Leave with integrity: give appropriate notice, do not sabotage, and keep a faithful testimony.

A pastoral word
The Westminster Standards press both holiness of heart and holiness of life. They call Christians to contentment and to avoid covetousness, but they also call us to exercise our lawful vocations faithfully and to steward resources. You can want legitimate improvement in your situation and act to obtain it without sinning — provided you guard your heart, examine motives, and act honestly in how you leave. Stealing a client list or confidential playbook to “even the score” is not a Christian way forward.

Integrity & Contentment Partnership Agreement
(An agreement of conscience and contract)

Preamble
We, the undersigned, Christian business partners who acknowledge our duties to God and neighbor as taught in the Westminster Standards — especially the biblical duties against covetousness, lying, and injustice and the obligations of stewardship, truthfulness, repentance, reconciliation, and charity — enter into this written covenant and contract to govern our joint business dealings. This Agreement is both a solemn Christian covenant and a legally binding partnership agreement intended to be enforced according to its terms.

We expressly state our purpose is to run the Partnership in a manner that serves our clients with excellence, protects one another’s rights, honors the church, and cultivates integrity and contentment in heart and practice.

Article I — Definitions
1.1 “Partnership” — the business entity owned and operated by the undersigned, as of the Effective Date.
1.2 “Partner” — either undersigned partner, singularly or jointly, as the context requires.
1.3 “Competing Venture” — any business, enterprise, or material economic activity that offers the same or substantially similar products or services as the Partnership within the geographic and market scope in which the Partnership actively conducts business at the time of the activity.
1.4 “Key Employee” — an employee whose annual compensation equals or exceeds [fill amount] or who holds managerial, technical, sales, or client-facing responsibility such that their departure would reasonably reduce Partnership revenues by [fill percentage, e.g., 10%+] within one year.
1.5 “Key Client” — a client or account that accounted for at least [fill percentage, e.g., 10%] of Partnership gross revenue in the most recent fiscal year or whose loss would reasonably reduce Partnership revenue materially.
1.6 “Net Profits” — Partnership profits after ordinary and necessary business expenses and depreciation, calculated according to generally accepted accounting principles as applied consistently, and as set forth on the Partnership’s books and records.
1.7 “Tithe” — ten percent (10%) of Net Profits, unless otherwise agreed in writing.

Article II — Term; Covenant Not to Compete or Accept Outside Offers
2.1 Term. This Agreement begins on the Effective Date and continues until the Partnership is dissolved in accordance with Article IX or this Agreement is amended or terminated in writing by signed agreement of the Partners.
2.2 Non-compete during the Partnership. While this Partnership exists and while either Partner remains a Partner, neither Partner shall (a) start, own, operate, or materially participate in a Competing Venture, nor (b) accept employment, consultancy, equity, or other offers that would create a conflict of interest with the Partnership or materially divert the Partner’s efforts from the Partnership’s affairs, without the prior written consent of the other Partner, which consent shall not be unreasonably withheld.
2.3 Remedies for breach. If a Partner breaches Section 2.2, the non-breaching Partner shall be entitled to any or all of the following remedies: injunctive relief to restrain competitive activity; an accounting of profits earned by the breaching Partner from the competing activity; disgorgement to the Partnership (or to the non-breaching Partner if the non-breaching Partner continues the business) of those profits; and, at the non-breaching Partner’s election, a buyout option as set out in Section 9.3. The non-breaching Partner may also pursue any other remedies available at law or in equity. The Partners acknowledge these remedies are reasonable and necessary to protect the Partnership.

Article III — Contentment, Resentment, and Monthly Confession
3.1 No harboring of resentment. The Partners covenant not to withhold love, kindness, or cooperation on the basis of resentment if one Partner receives a larger share or special compensation in a given year. Such differential distributions or allocations may occur for legitimate business reasons (e.g., additional, documented work, one-time contributions, or other agreed circumstances).
3.2 Monthly meeting and confession. The Partners will meet at least once each month for a meeting that includes: financial review, prayer, and a time for mutual confession and reconciliation. Any Partner who feels resentful concerning distributions, responsibilities, or conduct shall confess that resentment at the monthly meeting, describe the matter with charity and clarity, and submit to prayerful reconciliation. Minutes of the meeting shall record the confession and any agreed steps for resolution.
3.3 Failure to confess. If a Partner refuses to bring a confessed grievance to the monthly meeting or to engage in the reconciliation process in good faith, the other Partner may call for biblically-based mediation in accordance with Article VII. Persistent, unrepentant breach of the covenant of mutual forbearance may be grounds for dissolution or buyout under Article IX.

Article IV — Recruitment of Competitors’ Personnel and Clients; Split of Gains
4.1 Permitted recruitment with shared gain. If either Partner, in the course of legitimate business and by offering more compensation or fees than a competitor, hires away a Key Employee or secures a Key Client from a competitor, the Partners agree that the economic benefit attributable to that hire or client shall be shared equally (50/50), subject to the formula below.
4.2 Measurement of gain. “Gain” for this purpose shall be the incremental Net Profits of the Partnership directly attributable to the Key Employee or Key Client for the first twenty-four (24) months following the hire or client acquisition, less reasonable recruiter expenses and initial integration costs, as calculated by an independent CPA if the Partners cannot agree on amount. If the acquisition or hire directly creates a new product line or materially alters how revenue is derived, the Partners will in good faith agree on a measurement period and formula; absent agreement, an independent CPA shall determine attributable incremental Net Profits.
4.3 Timing of split. The Partner who procured the hire or client shall account to the Partnership within thirty (30) days of having documentation that the hire/client is secured and shall begin distribution of the other Partner’s share on the next regular distribution date, subject to the Partnership’s working capital needs and consistent accounting practices.

Article V — Books, Records, and Access
5.1 Honest books. The Partners shall keep full, accurate, and honest books, records, invoices, and accounts, prepared according to generally accepted accounting principles and the Partnership’s standard practices.
5.2 Access. Each Partner shall have full access at reasonable times to inspect books, records, contracts, communications, and digital accounts of the Partnership and to receive copies upon reasonable request. A refusal to permit such access is a material breach of this Agreement.
5.3 Annual audit. The Partners shall engage an independent CPA to conduct an annual review (or audit if required by law or the Partners agree) of the Partnership’s financial statements. The cost of such audit shall be a Partnership expense.

Article VI — Truthful Competition and Fair Dealing
6.1 No false claims. Neither Partner shall knowingly make false or disparaging statements about a competitor’s product or services, nor shall either engage in deceptive, fraudulent, or unlawful marketing practices. All advertising and representations must be truthful, verifiable, and presented with due respect for competitors, in keeping with the Biblical and Westminster insistence upon truth and neighborly love.
6.2 Retraction and remedy. If a Partner makes a false or misleading claim (knowingly or negligently), that Partner shall promptly retract the statement, publicly correct it if necessary, and make restitution for any proven harm caused to a competitor or third party. Failure to do so shall constitute a material breach subject to the remedies in Article IX.

Article VII — Disputes, Reconciliation, and Arbitration
7.1 Biblical first steps. In all disputes arising under this Agreement the Partners covenant to follow Matthew 18:15–17 and the principles of mutual discipline and reconciliation as set forth in Scripture and reflected in the Westminster Standards. Before initiating litigation or arbitration, the complaining Partner shall notify the other in writing and request a meeting for private resolution. If private resolution fails, the Partners shall present the matter to the elders (or recognized leaders) of [name of home church] or another mutually agreed Christian conciliation body for attempted biblical mediation.
7.2 If reconciliation fails. If the matter cannot be resolved through the church conciliation or if the parties do not agree on a church body, the dispute shall be finally resolved by binding arbitration under the rules of [chosen arbitration forum — e.g., American Arbitration Association] and conducted by a single arbitrator with commercial and, if possible, Christian mediation/arbitration experience. The arbitration shall be in [city/state to be filled], and judgment upon the award may be entered in any court having jurisdiction.
7.3 Emergency relief. Nothing in this Article precludes a Partner from seeking immediate injunctive or other emergency equitable relief from a court to prevent irreparable harm (for example, to prevent disclosure of confidential information or to stop a competing venture) pending arbitration, provided the dispute is submitted to arbitration thereafter.

Article VIII — Tithing and Use of Tithe
8.1 Tithe before salary. Before drawing salaries or distributions, the Partnership shall set aside the Tithe (10% of Net Profits) each fiscal year and remit it to gospel work as the Partners jointly direct.
8.2 Designation. The Partners shall agree annually on the recipient ministries or gospel work in keeping with orthodox Christian doctrine. The Partners may make interim commitments in consultation with each other, and payment shall be timely.
8.3 Accountability. Receipts and documentation of tithe distribution shall be kept as Partnership records and reviewed at the monthly meeting.

Article IX — Remedies, Buyout, and Dissolution
9.1 Remedies for material breach. Material breach of this Agreement gives the non-breaching Partner the right to seek remedies as provided here and at law or in equity, including specific performance, injunctive relief, accounting, and damages.
9.2 Events permitting dissolution. The Partnership may be dissolved by mutual written agreement, by operation of law, or upon (a) a material, unrepented breach of this Agreement that is not cured within thirty (30) days after written notice and reconciliation efforts through Articles III and VII, or (b) other events agreed by the Parties.
9.3 Buyout rights. On a declared dissolution or following a breach described in Section 9.2, the non-breaching Partner shall have the option to purchase the breaching Partner’s interest. The purchase price shall be the fair market value of the Partner’s interest as determined by an independent business valuation (or by mutual written agreement). If the breach was a willful violation of Article II, the non-breaching Partner may elect a buyout at fair market value discounted by twenty-five percent (25%) in recognition of breach-induced harm; the Partners will then proceed to close the transaction within sixty (60) days of valuation, or as otherwise agreed. The Parties may choose alternative buyout formulas in writing at any time.
9.4 Accounting upon dissolution. On dissolution, the Partnership shall wind up affairs, pay creditors, distribute reserves, pay the agreed tithe, and distribute remaining assets per capital accounts and prior agreements, subject to obligations hereunder.

Article X — Representations, Warranties, and Covenants
10.1 Each Partner represents and warrants that (a) they are entering this Agreement voluntarily and with full authority to bind themselves; (b) they are of sound mind; (c) they have disclosed any material conflicts or material outside commitments; and (d) the obligations herein reflect their sincerely held Christian convictions and their commitment to live by the moral principles reflected in the Westminster Standards.
10.2 Each Partner covenants to act in good faith, with mutual forbearance and fairness, to give timely notice of matters affecting the Partnership, and to prioritize the Partnership’s welfare within the bounds of conscience and lawful duty.

Article XI — Confidentiality; Public Statements
11.1 Confidential Information. Each Partner shall keep confidential all non-public Partnership information and shall not disclose it to third parties except as required by law or with prior written consent.
11.2 Public statements. Public statements about Partnership affairs, disputes, or finances shall be made only by mutual consent or by the Partner designated by mutual consent, except as required by law.

Article XII — Miscellaneous
12.1 Governing law. This Agreement shall be governed by and construed under the laws of [State/Country — fill in], without reference to conflict-of-law rules that would apply another jurisdiction’s laws.
12.2 Entire agreement; amendment. This Agreement is the entire agreement between the Partners concerning the matters herein and supersedes prior understandings. It may be amended only by a written instrument signed by both Partners.
12.3 Severability. If any provision is held invalid, the remainder of the Agreement shall continue in full force and effect.
12.4 Costs. The Partnership shall pay reasonable costs incurred for any required valuation or accounting, unless a Partner’s willful breach caused the dispute, in which case that Partner shall bear those reasonable costs.
12.5 Attestation of conscience. The Partners agree that the obligations in this Agreement are matters of conscience and that they will seek to live by them before God. Household Media Rule — Covenant of Our Home

Preamble
We are a covenant family under Christ, called to live out His Word in all things. The Westminster Confession and Catechisms teach that God requires us to keep His Sabbaths, to worship Him aright, to instruct and govern our household, and to walk in justice and truth toward our neighbors. With that conviction, and in love for one another’s souls, we enter this Household Media Rule and agree to keep it together. We bind ourselves to this not as legalism but as loving obedience and training in the fear of the Lord.

1. The Lord’s Day
- On the Lord’s Day (Sunday) we will not stream TV shows, watch films for entertainment, or play video games. This day is set apart for public and private worship, rest, family worship, instruction in God’s Word, and works of mercy as the Lord’s people ought. If special, sober edification (e.g., a Bible teaching video directly used for family worship) is necessary, it must be approved ahead of time by the parents.

(Reason: The Westminster Confession teaches that the Lord’s Day is to be sanctified for worship, rest, and Godly duties of family life.)

2. No Devices at the Table
- There will be no phones, tablets, consoles, or other devices at or during the family dinner table. Mealtimes are for nourishment, conversation, mutual encouragement, and the practice of gratitude and godly speech.

3. Media That Promotes Cruelty, Mockery of the Faith, or Sexual Immorality
- We will not watch films, programs, or videos that glorify cruelty, mock or belittle the Christian faith, or contain sexually explicit material. The parents will evaluate content, taking substance and context into account. When in doubt, the parents’ judgment stands for the younger children; older children and teens must seek parental permission before viewing borderline content.

(Practice: We will pre-watch or consult trustworthy reviews for anything younger children might see; for older kids, we require prior discussion and parental approval.)

4. Worship Music and the Regulative Principle (clarified)
- We will listen to worship music only when it is consistent with Scripture and sound doctrine and when it directs the heart to God in a manner fitting for worship. Because God requires that worship be according to His Word, we will not use music that promotes doctrinal error, licentiousness, or profane approaches to worship.
- That said, the Westminster Standards require worship to be according to the Word, but they do not simply declare all music from other Reformed or non-denominational churches inherently sinful. Therefore, we will not adopt a blanket rule that forbids all music produced outside our local denomination merely because it is from another body. Instead, we will judge each piece or artist by doctrine and practice: if an artist or church promotes false doctrine or unbiblical worship, we will not use their music in our family worship or regular listening; if an outside artist’s work is biblically faithful and edifying, the parents may permit it.

(Reason: The Regulative Principle requires that worship be ordered by Scripture; it does not, in itself, require isolation from every outside church’s musical expression if that expression is faithful to Scripture.)

5. Subscriptions and Stewardship (clarified)
- We will obtain and use digital media (streaming services, music platforms) honestly and lawfully. If the family uses a shared login, it must be authorized for our household use and used in a way that does not violate the provider’s terms or deprive another of his rightful property. We will not participate in or encourage large-scale unauthorized sharing of accounts that the service or owner has not permitted.
- If a relative (such as my brother) voluntarily and lawfully provides us a login for our household, and that sharing is within the service’s rules and the owner’s consent, we may use that account for our household. We will not, however, treat unauthorized mass sharing as acceptable on the basis that “companies overcharge.” Justice and truth require we respect others’ property and agreements.

(Reason: The confession and catechisms uphold obedience to the moral law, including honesty and not taking another’s goods; we must steward our resources and respect lawful ownership.)

6. Pre-watching and Reviews for Younger Children
- The parents will pre-watch or consult reliable reviews before younger children are allowed to watch any new show or film. Nothing is passed to them without parental approval. Older children may request permission and must discuss content beforehand.

Accountability and Consequences
- This is a household covenant. Parents will teach, model, and enforce the Rule with patience and consistency. Consequences for disobedience will be corrective and proportionate: conversation and instruction for minor slips; temporary loss of media privileges for repeated or willful disobedience; restoration upon repentance and agreement to the Rule.
- We will review this covenant together every six months, and parents will communicate any changes in writing. Major exceptions (e.g., for family outreach, school projects, or pastorally necessary reasons) require prior parental approval.

What the Westminster Standards require (brief)
- The eighth and ninth commandments demand honesty and restitution. The Shorter Catechism teaches that the eighth commandment requires us to preserve and restore what is another’s (we may not unjustly hinder our neighbor’s estate). Deliberate deception to obtain money is therefore wrong and calls for making restitution to those wronged.
- Repentance is more than sorrow; the Westminster Confession (ch. 15) and the Catechisms teach that genuine repentance includes confession, forsaking the sin, and, where possible, making reparation for the wrong done. Where sin has been public or has caused public scandal, public acknowledgement and repair are fitting.

So: quietly giving the money to charity in your own name does not meet the obligation to those you deceived. Donating can be a good thing, but it does not replace restoring what you took by false pretenses. You should (1) confess to God and seek the church’s pastoral counsel, (2) cease the practice (already done), (3) make a candid disclosure to those you deceived and offer restitution, and (4) follow through with transparent repayment.

Practical plan you can enact now

1) Get pastoral and legal counsel
- Talk first with a pastor/elder for spiritual oversight and accountability in how you approach confession and restitution.
- Consult a lawyer (or consumer-regulation guidance) about potential legal obligations in your jurisdiction so you don’t inadvertently make statements that create legal risk.

2) Calculate precisely what is owed
- Itemize every client who paid for an “ancestral clearing” and the amounts and dates. The people to whom you must make restitution are those who specifically paid for that service under the false claims.

3) Decide your realistic repayment capacity
- Figure out how much cash you can commit to repayments monthly or as a lump sum (sell assets, use savings, take a small loan, restructure cashflow). The moral duty is to make restitution “as far as possible” without becoming fraudulent to others, so be honest and realistic about timing.

4) Make a clear, humble disclosure and offer
- Tell the clients the truth, apologize, and offer restitution. Because the sin was directed at many persons, public or group disclosure (email to all affected clients) is appropriate; do so humbly and without defensive language.
- Offer each person a choice: an immediate full refund (if you can pay that quickly for those who request it), or a full refund by an agreed installment schedule (pro rata), or—only if the client explicitly requests it—a donation instead of a refund. Do not assume donation on their behalf.

5) If you cannot refund everyone immediately, use a fair, transparent pro‑rata repayment plan
- Don’t pick and choose arbitrarily. Commit to a monthly payment amount you can sustain, and distribute each month’s payment pro rata according to each client’s share of the total owed.
- Example method:
  - Total owed = $30,000.
  - You commit to pay $1,500/month toward that total.
  - Each month you distribute that $1,500 among all claimants proportionally to what each paid, until fully repaid (this means everyone receives the same percentage back each month).
- Provide a clear timeline estimate (e.g., at $1,500/month, all would be repaid in ~20 months) and update clients monthly with receipts and a running balance.
- Put payments through a traceable method (bank transfer, check) and keep clear records.

6) Transparency and accountability
- Appoint an independent person (an elder, accountant, or trusted third party) to receive funds and to report to the claimants periodically. Make monthly statements public to the claimants so they see progress.

7) Follow-through and pastoral repair
- Confess to God and to your local church leaders. If some clients want pastoral reconciliation or conversation, make yourself available. Make practical amendments to your practice and public materials so nothing like this is repeated.

Why your original instinct to “just tithe the money and move on” is insufficient
- The Westminster teaching separates acts of mercy from acts of justice. Charity is good, but does not satisfy the duty to restore what was unjustly taken from specific persons. Only if each wronged individual voluntarily agrees to forego restitution may you redirect those funds elsewhere.
