I. Principles from the Westminster Standards (summary, not technical citation)
- Repentance is more than sorrow: it requires contrition, confession, and a real change of life, including restitution where harm has been done to our neighbour. The Standards insist that sins against others must be made right as far as possible.
- Where a person has sinned against specific people, confession ought to be to those offended (not merely to God in private). Public scandal may call for public disclosure, but disclosure must be truthful and avoid rash judgment or slander.
- Christians are to be truthful, avoid false accusations, and submit to lawful civil procedures where appropriate.

Apply those general teachings as follows.

II. What you actually owe (numbers and reasoning)
Facts you gave:
- The pricier firm’s bid exceeded the cheapest by $18,000 total. That $18,000 was carried pro rata by the 40-unit association, i.e., $18,000/40 = $450 per unit.
- You received a “free” deck valued about $9,000 from the pricier firm.

Two ways people sometimes think about the money:
- “What did I personally unjustly gain?” — that is $9,000 benefit minus the $450 of the extra cost you yourself paid = $8,550 net personal unjust enrichment.
- “What harm did I cause the other owners?” — the other 39 owners bore $18,000 minus your $450 share = $17,550 of extra cost.

The Westminster principle emphasizes making right the injury to your neighbour. To restore the owners to the position they would have been in but for your misconduct, you should make good the loss borne by the other owners. That means restoring $17,550 to the association (or otherwise ensuring the 39 other owners are reimbursed). Because you also personally received unjust benefit, paying only your net unjust enrichment ($8,550) would not make the other owners whole — it would only disgorge your gain. So the morally correct restitution to repair the social injury is $17,550.

Practical options you might offer the board (choose one and be explicit when you confess):
- Offer to pay $17,550 to the HOA so the board can allocate refunds or credits to the other owners, or

III. Confession, naming Trevor, and investigation
- Confess to the board and to those offended. The Standards teach confession to offended parties as part of repentance.
- Do not make a public allegation that Trevor “cooked the books” unless you actually have clear evidence. The Ninth Commandment and the Standards condemn rash judgment and slander. If the paperwork shows Trevor signed or wrote the side-deck item, say that factually: “The side-deck work is documented on the contractor’s paperwork and appears to have been prepared by Trevor, an estimator at the company.” Offer the documents and ask the board to investigate. Your duty is to be truthful and avoid slander; your duty is also to seek the protection of the innocent and the rights of the wronged.

IV. The elevator vote and your “prophetic” duty
- You have a duty to speak truthfully and to warn your neighbors of real danger or fraud. But that must be done within the bounds of love, truth, and prudence: do not charge the board with “corruption” unless you have evidence. Public denunciation without proof can become another sin.

Those actions are both faithful and constructive; they preserve your conscience without making unproven slanderous charges.
- Do not let a zeal for exposing wrong tempt you into creating scandal where none is proven. Repentance aims at repair, not spectacle.

1) What the Standards say about repentance (briefly)
- The Shorter Catechism defines “repentance unto life” as a saving grace in which a sinner, “out of a true sense of his sin, and apprehension of God’s mercy in Christ, doth, with grief and hatred of his sin, turn from it unto God, with full purpose of, and endeavor after new obedience.” (Shorter Catechism, Q. 87)
- The Westminster teaching consistently connects genuine repentance with confession, godly sorrow for sin, and a sincere purpose of amendment. Repentance is not merely inward remorse; it issues in concrete acts to undo or repair wrongs and to obey God’s law toward our neighbor.

Apply those principles to your situation

A. The basic moral requirement: make restitution to those you wronged
- You deliberately took money by a false line item. That is theft/deceit with respect to your tenants’ property. The Standards require that repentance include not only sorrow but reparation: return what you wrongfully took to the rightful owners so far as you can.
- Practically: identify exactly how much each tenant was overcharged, and refund that amount. Include what is necessary to make them whole — at minimum the principal wrongly taken; many Christians, out of justice and charity, also include reasonable compensation for the deprivation (interest or an extra amount) as evidence of sincere repentance.

B. Confess to those you offended
- Genuine repentance normally includes confessing your wrong to those offended. That means telling each of the four tenants you added a false surcharge, apologizing, and offering restitution. This is painful and may have consequences (they may leave, be angry, or involve others), but the Standards teach that obedience and justice take priority over preserving reputation or profit.

C. The two tenants who moved away
- You should make diligent attempts to contact them and offer restitution. Send letters to last known addresses, emails, certified mail, phone if possible, and document your efforts. If after reasonable, documented attempts you cannot find them, keep a clear record and set the funds aside for them (or for their heirs) so that you have done what you could. Don’t simply ignore them and spend the money elsewhere without attempting to restore it.

D. Denise and the legitimately unpaid rent
- Your wrongful surcharge and Denise’s legitimate delinquent rent are distinct matters. Repentance requires you to return money you took by deceit. Forgiving Denise’s legitimate $900 rent is a separate, gracious act you may freely choose to do, but it is not required by repentance for your fraud. If you do forgive it, do so transparently and in writing so it is not a cover for not making proper restitution to others or to co-owners.
- If you forgive Denise’s debt, be sure her forgiveness does not mask or replace the refund she is owed from the surcharge; make both matters clear and separate when you speak with her.

E. The co-owner (Sam) and the $2,000 loan
- You cannot lawfully or ethically treat another person’s claim as cancelled without their consent. If the $2,000 is a legitimate claim by Sam or the partnership, your unilateral “forgiveness” would wrong him by taking his right to that repayment away. If you wish to forgive him as a personal act of charity, do so only with his informed agreement (and put it in writing).
- Also consider: if some of the money you took belonged in whole or part to Sam (as co-owner), restitution must account for his share. You must restore the rightful owner(s).

F. Don’t substitute secrecy or partial quiet fixes for full repentance
- Quietly giving a rent reduction to current tenants while ignoring the two former tenants does not meet the Standards’ demand for making wrongs right. Concealment or half-measures that avoid confession, restitution, and accountability are not genuine repentance.

G. Practical steps to take now (recommended)
1. Repent to God in prayer, confessing the sin specifically.
2. Prepare a clear accounting: list amounts taken per tenant, dates, and documentation.
3. Consult your co-owner and be transparent about the full accounting; agree how to handle any portion that belongs to him.
4. Contact each tenant personally, confess the wrongful surcharge, apologize, and offer payment of the exact amount taken (plus reasonable additional compensation if you choose). For those who moved, send certified letters and record your attempts.
5. If someone refuses restitution or cannot be found after reasonable effort, document that carefully and ask your pastor or session for counsel about next steps (and possibly consult an attorney about how to handle unclaimed funds legally).
6. If you decide to forgive any legitimate debts (Denise’s rent, or Sam’s loan), do so as a distinct, voluntary act and put it in writing; do not let “forgiving everything” be used to conceal failing to make restitution to those you cheated.
7. Bring this before your local church elders or a pastor for pastoral accountability and guidance in making things right and in ongoing repentance.

H. Legal and pastoral cautions
- The Standards also affirm submission to just civil law. There may be civil or even criminal consequences for deliberate financial fraud. You should consult an attorney to understand legal risks, while not using fear of legal consequences to avoid doing what is just.
- Involve your pastor/elders for spiritual counsel and accountability; they can help you carry through the difficult but necessary steps.

Conclusion (the pastoral summary)
True repentance, according to the Westminster Standards, is sorrow for sin plus a sincere, concrete turning from it. That requires confession and doing what you can to repair the injury — returning the money you wrongfully took to the tenants (or making documented, diligent effort to do so), being transparent with your co-owner about funds that belong to him, and only forgiving other legitimate claims as a separate, voluntary act of charity. Quiet concealment or sweeping everything away to “cleanse” your conscience is not genuine repentance. It will be costly, humbling, and disruptive — but that is the path Scripture and the Standards call us to when we have wronged our neighbor.

Short answer, in one sentence:
Faithfulness (per the Reformed/Westminster teaching) calls you to both mercy and prudence — restore the repentant where safe and appropriate, but only on clear, enforceable conditions that protect the theatre and its supporters and which the board can defend.

Why that answer follows the Standards (briefly)
- The Westminster teaching places great weight on repentance, restoration, and discipline together: wrongdoers are to be reclaimed when they truly repent, but ecclesiastical censures and safeguarding measures are appropriate until repentance is visible and proven in practice. Restoration is not the same as ignoring consequences or removing all safeguards. (See WCF Ch. 30 on church censures and the Scriptural pattern in Matt. 18; Gal. 6:1; 2 Cor. 2:6–8.)
- That framework yields two simultaneous duties: to practice charity and forgiveness toward a penitent person, and to exercise stewardship and wise governance to protect the common good. Both are moral requirements.

How to decide (recommended course of action)
1. Vote and policy basis
   - Convene the board to make a formal decision rather than leaving this ad hoc. Tie the decision to a clear, written policy for volunteers/returning workers with prior financial misconduct (so future cases are consistent).
   - If your bylaws require board approval for volunteer appointments or for safety/financial roles, follow that procedure.

2. Restore conditionally (recommended)
   - Permit Reggie to volunteer as a set-builder with explicit, written restrictions and a probationary period. This honors repentance and offers restoration while protecting the institution and donors. The key points:
     - No access to cash, ticketing systems, bookkeeping, or any financial records.
     - No keys, alarm codes, or unsupervised access to locked areas that contain funds, inventory, or sensitive materials.
     - Work only under an assigned supervisor who is briefed and agrees to the supervision.
     - A written volunteer agreement that lists restrictions, length of probation, reporting requirements, what constitutes breach, and immediate consequences (e.g., suspension or permanent ban).
     - Require continued participation in his recovery program and provide a contact person (mentor or sponsor) who can vouch for ongoing sobriety/repentance if appropriate.
     - Consider a background check or confirmation of restitution (you already have repayment, but document it).

3. Probation, review, and defined consequences
   - Set a clear probationary period (e.g., one season or six months with review at mid-point and end).
   - Establish objective criteria for successful completion (attendance, no relapse or policy breach, positive supervisor reports, continued recovery participation).
   - If any violation occurs, have an agreed immediate step (suspension pending board review, permanent ban if criminality recurs).
   - Document everything and keep records of the agreement and evaluations.

4. Communication plan
   - Do not stage a public “welcome back” until trust is demonstrably rebuilt and until key stakeholders (major donors, key board members) are satisfied with the safeguards and the outcome of the probation.
   - Be cautious with publicity: initial restoration should be quiet and pastoral, not heralded. Public celebrations can come later if warranted by demonstrated change.
   - For worried donors: offer a calm, factual explanation if necessary — state that restitution was made, that his return would be limited to non-financial duties under strict safeguards, and that the board adopted a written policy and oversight. Donors do not need detailed personal information, but they do need assurance that stewardship and safeguards are in place.
   - Avoid vilification of Reggie (uncharitable speech). Avoid false reassurance (don’t promise more than the board is prepared to enforce).

5. Reassure and bind the board
   - Ask the board to agree in advance to the safeguards and to the consequences if safeguards are violated, so no one is put in a position of acting alone.
   - If some board members cannot in conscience accept conditional restoration, make sure they understand the reasoning (Scriptural call to restore the penitent, plus prudential safeguards). If they still cannot agree, consider whether their opposition is to the principle of restoration itself or to some tactical detail; work to find mutually acceptable safeguards, and if necessary take a binding vote.

Practical/legal items to include
- Written volunteer agreement (restrictions, probation, monitoring, consequences).
- Assigned supervisor and reporting line.
- Documented restitution on file (you already have this; keep it accessible).
- Liability check: confirm with your insurer or counsel whether a volunteer with prior misconduct raises coverage issues.
- A formal “re-entry” policy for future comparable situations so the board can rely on precedent.

Pastoral tone and moral reasoning to present to the board
- Remind the board of the twin obligations: to show mercy to a repentant person and simultaneously to protect the theatre’s patrons, donors, and mission.
- Use the Westminster pattern: discipline is for reclaiming (not only punishment). If Reggie’s repentance is sincere, restoration is proper — but restoration in the Reformed tradition is often gradual and conditional until repentance is proven in practice.
- Allow space for those still wounded: suggest opportunities for them to meet privately with leadership to express concerns and to receive reassurance about safeguards.

What to expect and how to handle fallout
- Some donors or board members may remain unhappy. Be honest: restoration of a person will not erase hurt; you cannot please everyone. But you can show you acted prudently, documented safeguards, and respected both mercy and stewardship.
- If a donor threatens withdrawal, try private conversation: explain policy and controls, offer reporting on the probation, and, if necessary, accept that some will not return. That hazard does not justify either unconditional reentry without safeguards or permanent exclusion when repentance has occurred.

Sample brief terms (you can adapt)

- Supervised at all times; assigned supervisor signs to confirm compliance.
- Mandatory continued attendance in recovery program; provide contact info of sponsor or counselor.
- Three-month probation with a formal review at 6 weeks and at 3 months; unilateral suspension for any breach.
- No public announcement for the duration of probation.

Conclusion
The Westminster standards require both restoration and churchly discipline: restore the penitent, but do so prudently with safeguards until repentance is proved. Practically, that points to a conditional, supervised re-entry with a clear written agreement and board oversight, no public fanfare while on probation, and a communications strategy to reassure donors. That approach is morally faithful, defensible to donors, and gives Reggie a legitimate path back without endangering your organization.

Grounding from the Westminster Standards

1) The controlling principle — worship only as God has appointed
- WSC Q54 (exact quote): “What is required in the second commandment? The second commandment requireth the receiving, observing, and keeping pure and entire all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath appointed in his Word; and doth forbid the worshipping of God by images, or any other way not appointed in his Word.”

This question and answer should be your first rule of thumb. It requires that worship and ordinances be those God has appointed in Scripture and forbids worship “by images, or any other way not appointed” in God’s Word.

2) The same standard applied consistently rules out private revelation but does not automatically outlaw all human means of creating atmosphere
- WCF 21.1 (on the rule for acceptable worship): “The acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, nor the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the holy Scripture.” (WCF 21 is the chapter dealing with Religious Worship; this clause insists worship must be instituted by God’s revealed will and not according to human devices.)

Taken together, these texts require that worship be commanded or warranted by Scripture and forbid image‑worship and human inventions that amount to unauthorized worship. That is why you rightly appeal to the second commandment where the danger is genuine.

How those clauses apply to your two rulings

- Ruling 1 (keep the 40‑minute guided meditation that tells people to picture Jesus vividly and receive “affirmations back ‘from him’” and then an altar): The Westminster standard cautions against “any other way not appointed in his Word.” If the practice is presented as merely a devotional imagination exercise shaped by Scripture (e.g., imagining Christ’s parable scenes while meditating on a specific text, with clear instruction that any feelings or “words” are to be tested by and subordinate to Scripture and pastoral oversight), it can be permissible. But if the exercise instructs people to treat felt impressions as direct, personal, authoritative words from Jesus—especially as the basis for altar responses—that risks “worship…in any other way not appointed in his Word” and may imply private revelation or image‑like representation. The Westminster standard requires caution: devotional exercises must be subordinate to Scripture and not put inward impressions on the same level as God’s Word.

If you keep it, reframe and restrain it: root every step in a specific Scripture passage, instruct participants that impressions are to be tested and not equated with Scripture, and provide pastoral safeguards (clear teaching beforehand, disclaimers in the mediation script, follow‑up debrief). - Ruling 2 (ban the acoustic‑guitar instrumental prelude and the warm low lighting as “man‑made mood manufacturing”): The second commandment forbids unlawful images and invented rites of worship; it does not entail that every human means that shapes atmosphere is ipso facto forbidden. Instrumental music, lighting, etc., are not in themselves images worshipping God, nor necessarily “other way not appointed” if used as circumstances of worship ordered to Scripture, done under pastoral oversight, and not treated as magical means to coerce feeling or replace sound doctrine. The standards distinguish between worship elements appointed by God (preaching, sacraments, prayer, praise) and the lawful “circumstances” and adiaphora that can be used, so long as they are not treated as substitutes for Scripture or as constituting an unauthorized form of worship.

Therefore: a blanket ban is not the straightforward implication of WSC Q54/WCF 21.1. Instead, apply the same test you should apply to the meditation: are these practices (a) explicitly taught or warranted in Scripture, or (b) lawful circumstances ordered to promote the ends of Scriptural worship without substituting feelings or private revelations for doctrine? If yes, they may be permitted; if they become a vehicle for invented ritual or emotionally manipulative practice presented as normative or sacramental, they should be restricted.

Short answer up front

- No — you may not “put into” the church’s public, corporate worship practices that are not instituted by Christ or his apostles (the regulative principle). The Westminster Confession expressly limits acceptable worship to what God has revealed. (WCF 21.1)
- Also: you should not cavalierly abolish venerable practices affecting conscience and devotion without scriptural warrant, careful pastoral teaching, and the church’s due order. The Standards protect the conscience from human impositions and require charity and prudence in matters not expressly commanded. (WCF 20.2; see guidance below for how to handle both halves practically.)

The governing texts (quoted)

- WCF 21.1 — Of Religious Worship: “The acceptable way of worshiping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshiped according to the imaginations and devices of men, nor the suggestions of Satan, under any visible representation, or any other way not prescribed in the Holy Scripture.”
- WCF 20.2 — Of Christian Liberty: “God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men, which are in anything contrary to his Word, or beside it, in matters of faith or worship, so as to deny his Word, or require an implicit faith, and blind obedience unto men.”

How those texts apply to what you propose

1) Part 1 — “What we ADD” (labyrinth, centering breath-prayer borrowed from another tradition, an annual ashes-and-oil anointing rite)

- The Confession’s plain rule in WCF 21.1 is the decisive principle for corporate worship: public worship must be “instituted by himself” (i.e. Christ/God in Scripture) and limited to what Scripture prescribes. If a practice is presented as an element of the church’s public worship, and it has no clear warrant in Scripture (by command, example of the apostles, or necessary consequence), the Confession treats additions as disallowed.
- That means you cannot properly introduce practices into the congregation’s corporate liturgy simply because Scripture does not explicitly forbid them. The Confession does not license “anything not forbidden”; it requires the reverse: only what is prescribed is to be performed in worship.
- Practically: a labyrinth walk, a centering breath-prayer borrowed from a non‑Christian (or different) tradition, or a novel anointing rite (presented as a corporate worship rite) are the kinds of innovations WCF 21.1 warns against unless you can show clear scriptural institution. Particularly where a practice is borrowed from another religion or tradition, the Confession’s warning against worship “according to the imaginations and devices of men” is weighty.

Pastoral alternative for Part 1 (consonant with the Standards)
- Don’t fold these practices into the church’s official, corporate worship service without careful theological grounding and the church’s authority. You can consider offering such things as optional, clearly-labelled devotional opportunities (e.g., a Lenten devotional station, an educational/discipleship group on centering prayer with critical instruction, a pastoral-care anointing service for the sick following James 5 taught carefully), but avoid making them a part of the Lord’s Day corporate service unless you can show scriptural warrant and gain church agreement.

2) Part 2 — “What we BAN” (abolish kneeling during confession, ten seconds of silence, fixed 10:30 start)

- The Confession’s regulative principle (WCF 21.1) does argue against inventing new public rites; but it does not give an automatic license to abolish every human practice that lacks an explicit New Testament command. Some practices are “circumstances” or pastoral prudence (posture for prayer, silence to prepare hearts, a set start time) and others are matters touching conscience and worship that the Standards handle under Christian liberty.
- WCF 20.2 protects the conscience from being bound by men in matters of faith or worship that are “beside” Scripture. That works two ways: you should not impose unscriptural forms on consciences; nor should you rigidly forbid devotions (like kneeling in confession) that are not sinful and are pastoral aids to devotion, unless there is clear biblical reason.
- Thus, summarily abolishing kneeling, silence, or a known start time risks ruling by personal preference where Scripture gives room for conscience and pastoral prudence. The Standards call for care, not caprice.

Pastoral alternative for Part 2 (consonant with the Standards)
- Treat postures or brief silences as adiaphora (things indifferent) so long as they are not sinful and do not contravene Scripture; do not unilaterally forbid them. If a practice causes public scandal or clearly obstructs the worship of the congregation, address that particular pastoral concern, teach the congregation the biblical reasons for a change, and seek the church’s ordered decision.
- If you wish to change the order (e.g., start time), do so transparently, with teaching and consultation through the church’s recognized process (session/elders/vestry), not by fiat from a planning team.

A few concrete, Standards‑shaped recommendations

- Before adding any new rite to corporate worship, require (and put in writing) a scriptural/theological rationale show­ing how the rite is instituted by Scripture (command, apostolic example, or necessary inference). WCF 21.1 is the standard you must meet.
- If an item is devotional or educational and lacks direct warrant for corporate worship, offer it as an optional, clearly‑labelled ministry (Lenten weekday labyrinth, an adult education class on contemplative practices with critical, Reformed instruction, pastoral anointing for the sick per James 5).
- If you want to stop a common pastoral practice (kneeling, silence, start time), bring the change through the church’s governance and pastoral process, teach the congregation, and protect consciences (WCF 20.2). Seek unity and charity rather than unilateral abolition.
- When a practice is borrowed from another tradition, be especially cautious: the Confession warns against worship “according to the imaginations and devices of men” and against adopting forms that may carry theological meanings contrary to Reformed doctrine.

Conclusion

Your reasoning that “what Scripture does not forbid is permitted” is exactly backward from the Westminster rule for public worship. WCF 21.1 insists that corporate worship must be what God has appointed; therefore you may not lawfully introduce novel rites into the congregation’s worship without scriptural warrant and the church’s oversight. At the same time, WCF 20.2 protects conscience and requires pastoral prudence: do not abolish longstanding devotional practices lightly or impose new liturgical forms coercively. Proceed with biblical argument, pastoral sensitivity, and the church’s ordained processes.

Short answer: Neither side is entirely right when they cite the Standards as they’ve quoted them. The Westminster Standards affirm both (a) liberty of conscience and (b) that the manner of acceptable public worship must be appointed by God (i.e., determined by Scripture). You cannot appeal to the “freedom” clause to justify inventing new forms of corporate worship that are “beside” or contrary to God’s Word. Below I give the key texts and then practical counsel for how to proceed in your ministry.

Key texts (Westminster Confession of Faith)
- WCF 20.2 — “God alone is Lord of the conscience, and hath left it free from the doctrines and commandments of men which are in any thing contrary to his Word, or beside it, in matters of faith or worship.”
- WCF 21.1 — “The light of nature shows that there is a God, who has lordship and sovereignty over all; and is therefore to be worshipped: but the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men, or the suggestions of Satan, under the notion of worshipping God.”
- WCF 1.6 — “The whole counsel of God concerning all things necessary for his own glory, man’s salvation, faith and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture.”

How these texts bear on your situation
- The “freedom of conscience” passage (WCF 20.2) is not an unrestricted license to create new modes of public worship. It protects believers from human doctrines and commands that are contrary to or “beside” Scripture. That phrase (“beside it”) is the limiter: freedom applies only where men’s rules do not contravene the Word and are not adding to it in matters of faith or worship.
- The worship chapter (WCF 21.1) makes the complementary point: acceptable worship is instituted by God and limited by his revealed will, so worship “may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men.” That language plainly warns against inventing new, authoritative forms of worship for the church.
- WCF 1.6 underscores the test: what we believe and how we worship must be grounded in Scripture or necessarily deduced from it.

Practical implications and counsel
1. Don’t treat the “sensory encounter” rites as required or as constituting the church’s public worship if you can’t show biblical warrant.
   - The Standards distinguish between liberty and the regulation of public worship. If the incense walk, guided-imagery meditation of Christ’s face, or a self-authored “Spirit-fire” candle rite are presented as part of the congregation’s worship service (i.e., something the church does corporately as worship), the burden is to show that they are biblically warranted or at least not “beside” Scripture.

2. Test each element by Scripture and by the Standards’ principle.
   - Ask: Is this element commanded, exemplified, or necessarily derived from Scripture for public worship? If not, is it clearly a neutral adiaphoron that can safely be used without implying that worship is done differently than Scripture ordains?
   - Guided visualisation of Jesus, lighting candles, and incense have biblical imagery in places (e.g., Scripture uses fire, incense, and images of Christ), but the WCF requires care: using biblical imagery as teaching or devotional illustration is different from instituting new liturgical acts as corporate worship.

3. Make such practices voluntary and clearly devotional if retained.
   - If you find pastoral value in sensory aids, consider using them in small-group devotionals, educational settings, or as optional participatory experiences outside the formal corporate worship service — and make participation clearly voluntary. That respects others’ consciences and avoids imposing a new corporate rite.

4. Engage the elders and older members in careful, charitable conversation.
   - The Standards expect church government and mutual accountability. Older members who object are not necessarily imposing an illegitimate “man-made rule” simply by appealing to WCF 21.1; they are appealing to the Reformed principle that public worship must conform to God’s revealed will. Present your rationale (Scriptural reasons, pastoral aims, safeguards), listen to theirs, and seek a biblically faithful middle way.

5. Avoid sacramental language or veneration tied to invented rites.
   - If candles, incense, or imagery are given sacramental or mystical status in your practice (e.g., treated as means that effect grace), that would raise further concerns under the Standards. Keep such practices clearly pedagogical or devotional, not constitutive of the sacraments or the means of grace.

Conclusion
WCF 20.2 does not give you a free pass to invent corporate worship practices that are “beside” Scripture; WCF 21.1 confirms that corporate worship must be appointed by God. You are right that conscience is to be free from mere human traditions that contradict Scripture, but the Standards also require that public worship be governed by Scripture, not by private invention. My counsel: test your rites against Scripture, make them optional and clearly devotional if you keep them, and work with the elders and older members in a humble, scriptural dialogue rather than asserting that the “freedom clause” automatically trumpets every innovation.

Worship Standards — Key Section (draft)

Preface
Our denomination receives the teaching of the Westminster Confession of Faith and Catechisms as the faithful summary of biblical doctrine to which we submit. Two doctrines of special relevance to worship are (1) the sufficiency of Holy Scripture and (2) the manner in which acceptable worship is to be determined. The Confession declares the sufficiency of Scripture: “The whole counsel of God concerning all things necessary for His own glory, man’s salvation, faith and life, is either expressly set down in Scripture, or by good and necessary consequence may be deduced from Scripture” (WCF 1.6). The Confession likewise affirms the regulative principle: “The acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself, and so limited by his own revealed will, that he may not be worshipped according to the imaginations and devices of men” (WCF 21.1). These principles shape everything that follows.

1. The regulative principle and the limits of innovation
1.1 The congregation shall worship God only in the elements, words, and ceremonies that Christ has instituted or that are warranted by the Scriptures. Worship is not to be formed from private or public invention and presented as divinely instituted. (WCF 21.1; WCF chapters on the sacraments.)
1.2 In particular, no congregation or minister shall introduce rites or ordinances presented as sacraments or as conveying saving grace that are not the sacraments instituted by Christ in Scripture. The sacraments belong to the covenantal economy as instituted by Christ and are not open to the creation of novel sacraments by human authority. (See the Confession’s treatment of the sacraments.)
1.3 The careful and creative development of liturgy, music, and pastoral practice is permitted when it is subordinate to and consistent with the Word; but no such development may be represented as a new divine revelation or as replacing what God has plainly appointed. (WCF 1.6; WCF 21.1.)

2. Ecclesiastical order, rubrics, and discipline
2.1 The church has a biblical and confessional responsibility to keep order in public worship. To that end, sessions/consistories and assemblies may adopt rubrics and schedules to promote reverence, edification, and the orderly administration of the means of grace.
2.2 Such church regulations (for example: hymn selections, times of service, posture for particular acts of worship, or procedural sequences) are ecclesiastical rules binding under the church’s discipline and polity; they are not, however, equivalent to the divine revelation contained in Scripture. The adoption of a rubric therefore does not convert human ordinance into Scripture. (WCF 1.6.)
2.3 Where uniformity is required by denominational polity, those rules should be stated as ecclesiastical standards that regulate order and unity; discipline may be applied for wilful, unrepentant breach of those rules insofar as they are part of the church’s commanded order, but penalties presume a distinction between human ordinance and God’s own revealed commands. The church must be careful not to anathematize conscience or call a purely human disciplinary matter “sin against God’s revealed will” unless Scripture itself has so commanded.

3. Practical application to matters often in dispute
3.1 On hymns and music: The denomination may recommend or require certain hymnals or a range of hymn numbers as part of denominational unity; such requirements should be advanced as ecclesiastical polity, not as new articles of faith or as equal to Scripture. If a congregation departs from denominational hymn rules, the response should be governed by church discipline and pastoral correction, not by asserting that such departures are a crime against Scripture.
3.2 On posture and liturgical gestures: Decisions about kneeling, standing, or other postures for corporate acts (prayer, confession, sacrament) may be provided in denominational rubrics to promote reverence and unity. These postures are legitimate means to foster devotion but are not themselves matters of salvation or biblical command apart from explicit Scriptural warrant. They should therefore be enforced as ecclesiastical norms in a manner consistent with charity and pastoral care.
3.3 On service times: Reasonable rules about start times and punctuality are proper exercises of church order. A denomination may encourage or require standard service times for the sake of pastoral planning and congregational life; such rules are administrative, and deviation should be addressed in the same terms as other matters of church order rather than by declaring such deviation to be on par with violating Scripture.

4. Application of discipline and pastoral temper
4.1 Where the church’s polity prescribes specific rubrics (e.g., a denominational hymnal or set service elements), ministers and sessions must teach those rubrics as binding within that polity and apply discipline for obstinate refusal to conform. However, the church must not equate such refusals with the denial of core doctrine or declare them to be a breach of God’s revealed will unless that is truly the case on Scriptural grounds.
4.2 Pastoral patience, catechesis based on the Larger and Shorter Catechisms, and correction with a view to restoration should be the norm in administering discipline about worship practices that are principally ecclesiastical.

Concluding affirmation
We submit worship practice to the judgment of God’s Word, as the Westminster Standards require: Scripture provides the rule of worship and the Confession prevents the church from making either private invention or ecclesiastical regulation into a rival to God’s revelation. We therefore reject both extremes — the unchecked invention of rites and sacraments as though they were divine, and the elevation of mere ecclesiastical rubrics into divine law equal to Scripture — while affirming the church’s responsibility to foster order, reverence, and unity by serious but biblically proportioned rules and discipline. (WCF 1.6; WCF 21.1.)

2) Prayer of invocation and thanksgiving — pastor leads the congregation in prayer, giving thanks to God for the lives of our departed brothers and sisters
3) Singing — hymns and songs that point to Christ’s comfort and resurrection hope (team-led)
4) Scripture reading (selected passage on resurrection, comfort, Christian hope)
5) Preaching — the Word of God (kept central; sermon to apply Scripture pastorally to grief, hope, and Christian remembrance)
6) Corporate prayer — pastor and elder lead; include specific prayer for families who have lost loved ones

8) Pastoral benediction and dismissal
9) After the service — opportunity for pastoral care in the fellowship area; families may greet one another; any cultural foods or music for fellowship are permitted in the reception area after the service, at the discretion of leadership, provided they are not presented as part of the church’s worship liturgy.

Team expectations (binding)
- Do not permit or facilitate any practice in the sanctuary during the worship service that invites the dead to intercede, that treats images as objects of worship, or that introduces rites (incense, ritual offerings, prayers to saints) that are not part of our Scriptural worship.

Preamble — Our Purpose and Promise
We are four brothers/sisters, Christians bound together by the gospel, and we make this covenant before God and one another for the express purpose of honoring our mother, preserving family peace, and mortifying the sins of covetousness, envy, and dishonor. We do this in reliance upon Scripture and in the spirit of the covenant life commended in our faith — to love, to bear one another’s burdens, to confess and restore one another in brotherly/sisterly discipline, and to honor our parents with thankful hearts.

Therefore, in the fear of the Lord and to keep one another accountable, we freely and solemnly enter this Family Contentment & Honor Covenant with the following terms, to remain in force while our mother is living.

Article I — Proximity of Care
1.1 None of us shall accept employment, promotion, or a permanent move that places our ordinary residence or primary place of work more than one hour’s travel from our mother’s home (one hour measured by the reasonable driving time under ordinary traffic conditions), so long as she lives. We acknowledge that choosing career gain at the cost of forsaking our filial duty is covetousness and dishonor we covenant against.

1.2 In an extraordinary, unforeseeable emergency (medical, economic, or other serious cause), a sibling who believes they must be away for a limited, specified period will notify the other siblings in writing immediately and seek the unanimous consent of the others for the absence. Absent unanimous consent, the proposed absence is a breach of this covenant.

Article II — Monthly Heart-Examination and Accountability
2.1 Each month on our agreed family call, each sibling shall perform a brief, public examination of conscience before the group: naming aloud any stirring of envy, covetousness, or resentment toward another sibling for any favor, gift, or responsibility shown that year.

2.2 When any sibling names such a stirring, they shall (a) confess it, (b) describe in plain terms how it is manifesting in thought, word, or action, and (c) accept and receive counsel, admonition, prayer, and a concrete accountability plan from the group until that sin is put to death.

2.3 This monthly practice is a binding spiritual discipline while our mother lives. No sibling may opt out. Refusal to participate is itself a breach requiring remedial steps in Article VIII (Remedy & Restoration).

Article III — Caregiving and Testamentary Reminder
3.1 Each year we will note who has performed the preponderance of the hands-on caregiving for our mother. That sibling is entitled to a private, respectful opportunity to remind our mother, in their own words and never in a manipulative or coercive way, of the burdens they have borne, using the agreed phrase if they wish: “Those who carry the weight should be remembered accordingly,” at a time when our mother is independently reviewing her affairs.

3.2 Such private reminders must be kindly offered, never insistent, and must not cross the line into pressure, guilt, or deception (see Article V).

Article IV — Shared Ledger of Expenses
4.1 We will keep one shared, honest ledger that records every expense any sibling incurs on behalf of our mother’s care (medical costs, out-of-pocket caregiving expenses, travel directly for care, supplies, etc.). The ledger will be maintained in an accessible digital format (e.g., cloud spreadsheet) with receipts attached when practicable and be open to the review of any sibling at any time.

4.2 Ledger administration will rotate annually among the siblings. Any disputes about entries will be raised at the next monthly call and resolved by consensus or, if necessary, by referral to the agreed church elder or adviser named in Article VII.

Article V — No Pressure, No Guilt, No Deception of Our Mother
5.1 No sibling shall pressure, guilt, threaten, mislead, or deceive our mother regarding her money, her will, or any matter of disposition or giving. We regard such conduct as sinful and contrary to honoring a parent. If a sibling is found to have violated this Article, they shall confess, make restitution where appropriate, and submit to the discipline and restoration process in Article VIII.

Article VI — Tithing of Inheritances to Gospel Work
6.1 For the sake of gratitude and to guard against covetousness, each sibling commits that, from anything they individually inherit from our mother (but not from pre-existing trusts or gifts she already designated before her death unless the sibling chooses), they will set aside and give at least ten percent (10%) to gospel ministry or charitable evangelistic and church-planting work of their choosing, and will notify the other siblings of the beneficiary ministries within a year of receipt.

6.2 If a sibling desires to give a greater portion, they are encouraged to do so. Our aim is not legalism but a thankful discipline that keeps our hearts rightly ordered.

Article VII — Oversight and Dispute Resolution
7.1 We regard this covenant as a moral and spiritual compact, to be enforced by conscience, mutual exhortation, prayer, and, if needed, churchly discipline. To that end, we agree to invite our local church elders (or a mutually agreed mature Christian counselor or pastor) to serve as impartial advisers if any dispute cannot be resolved among us within 30 days.

7.2 Any party may request that an elder be engaged; the elders’ role will be to hear, mediate, and, if required, pronounce a binding restoration path for those who have sinned against the covenant.

Article VIII — Remedy, Confession, and Restoration
8.1 A breach of this covenant is primarily a moral and spiritual offense among siblings. The immediate steps upon a credible breach are:
  - Honest confession by the offending sibling before the group,
  - A public apology to those offended and to our mother if appropriate,
  - A restitution plan where applicable (including financial restitution recorded in the ledger),
  - Concrete corrective actions and an accountability plan (frequency of check-ins, commitments about proximity, etc.) until the breach is healed.

8.2 If a sibling persists in breach without repentance after counsel and pastoral intervention, the other siblings may suspend certain discretionary family privileges (for example, exclusion from decision-making roles concerning additional discretionary distributions to which the siblings might otherwise have a say) until repentance and reconciliation are evident. Any such suspension will be implemented prayerfully and only after pastoral consultation.

Article IX — Duration, Amendment, Witness, and Signatures
9.1 This covenant is in force while our mother is living. Any term may be amended only by unanimous written agreement of all siblings and recorded as an amendment appended to this document.

9.2 We desire this covenant to be witnessed by one or more mature Christians (preferably an elder or pastor of our church) who will sign below to acknowledge they have witnessed our vow to one another.

9.3 We sign this covenant freely, without coercion, intending to bind our consciences before God and one another, asking the Lord for mercy, grace, humility, and perseverance to keep it.

Grounds from the Westminster Standards (plainly and honestly)
1) The governing principle: worship must be instituted by God in his Word, not devised by men.
- The Westminster Confession (Ch. XXI) teaches that "the acceptable way of worshipping the true God is instituted by himself" and that we must not add to the worship God has appointed. That is the regulative principle as set out in our Standards: public worship is ordered by Scripture, not by innovations or human inventions. Practices that claim spiritual efficacy apart from Scripture’s appointed means are forbidden.

2) Why Proposal One must be rejected.
- The Blessing Stone proposes a weekly rite (layers pressing a hand on a stone and receiving oil while a leader pronounces a release of blessing) and teaches that the stone and oil “carry” the blessing and that touching them is how grace is received.
- That is precisely the kind of human invention the Confession forbids: an added ritual that attributes saving or conveying power to an object or work and makes a tactile action the means by which God’s blessing is "claimed." It borders on superstition and sacramentizing an object; it can also coerce conscience by saying someone who does not participate is "leaving their breakthrough unclaimed."
- Scripture gives the Word, sacraments (as Christ instituted them), prayer, praise, and other means appointed by God. Nothing in Scripture commands or authorizes this kind of rite as part of public worship. For those reasons the practice is not permitted in a church bound to the Westminster standard.

3) Why Proposal Two is different and may be permitted (with conditions).
- The Confession and the Directory emphasize Scripture‑directed, reverent worship, and they include singing as part of public worship. Historically the Assembly stressed singing the Psalms; that history informs many Presbyterian churches’ practice (some of which practice exclusive psalmody). The Standards require that worship elements be scriptural.
- Replacing a paid choir anthem with congregational singing of new songs is not, on its face, a novel sacramental rite or a superstition. Congregational singing of doctrinally sound, God‑directed songs can be a legitimate form of worship so long as it does not contradict Scripture or the church’s adopted practice under the Standards.
- Therefore: if this congregation’s confessional practice requires exclusive psalmody (or the session and congregation have adopted the Directory in a way that limits singing to the Psalms), Proposal Two must be rejected as contrary to that adopted practice. If the session has not restricted singing to the Psalms, the session may lawfully permit new congregational songs — but it must do so carefully.

- Examine the lyrics and theology: none must contradict Scripture or teach error. Songs must be clearly biblical in content.
- Evaluate the form and order: they should be singable by the congregation, fit the liturgical flow, and be used with reverence and due order (no gimmicks, no coercion).
- Preserve due deference to the choir and to those who have labored in the choir ministry: involve them in the transition and provide opportunities for them to serve.

Short answer up front
- Under the Westminster Standards the moral law governs the heart as well as the life. The tenth commandment forbids covetousness, envy, grudging, and all sinful inward motions toward another’s good. So the decisive question is what is in the heart, not only what is done outwardly.

That initial temptation, if it was only a fleeting motion and was truly repented of, is not a continuing ten‑commandment breach; if it involved deliberate, delighted consent it would have been sin, but you say she renounced it. - Tom: though his outward behaviour is blameless, his settled inward resentment, secret hopes that Aisha stumble, and keeping a tally “in case it’s useful” are exactly the sort of inward corruptions the tenth commandment forbids. Why (in doctrinal terms)
- The Westminster teaching consistently insists that the law binds the conscience and the affections, and that sin includes inward acts of the mind and will as well as outward acts. The tenth commandment is not exhausted by outward theft or grasping; it forbids covetous desires, envy, grudging, and delighting in another’s hurt. Merely feeling a fleeting temptation is not the same as consenting to and cherishing that temptation; but deliberately nursing resentment or secretly rejoicing in another’s misfortune is sin of the heart.
- Thus the moral verdict rests primarily on the heart: honest repentance removes guilt; secret, settled malice is real guilt even if no outward offense appears.

Preamble
We are committed both to treating departing colleagues with charity and to speaking the truth. The Westminster standards teach that Christians must not lie, and yet must do good to our neighbor and avoid needlessly injuring another’s reputation. In that spirit, this policy requires written references to be charitable in tone and restrained in airing faults, while forbidding falsehood. Managers are accountable to this policy and must sign it before providing references on behalf of the firm.

Scope
This policy applies to all managers and others who provide written references, recommendations, or employment-verification letters on firm letterhead, whether given directly to a prospective employer, a background-check provider, or provided to the employee for their use.

Policy Rules (binding)
1. Omit negative assessments in routine written references.
   - A written reference must not mention an employee’s weaknesses, failures, or “growth areas,” even if true and privately known, unless:
     a) the departing employee has given a clear, written release authorizing disclosure of those matters; or
     b) disclosure is required by law or a court order; or
     c) the prospective employer has requested such information and the manager has confirmed (in writing) the employee’s authorization to disclose.
   - In ordinary circumstances managers should focus written references on duties performed, responsibilities held, accomplishments that are true and documentable, and strengths that genuinely apply.

2. Praise sincerely; do not assert what you know to be false.
   - Managers are expected to affirm and highlight genuine strengths of departing employees whenever those statements are true.
   - A manager must not state that an employee is “strong,” “a great hire,” or “highly recommended” if, in the manager’s honest judgment, that affirmative endorsement would be false.
   - If a manager cannot truthfully give an affirmative recommendation, the manager must either:
     a) provide a neutral, factual verification of employment (dates of employment, title(s), primary responsibilities, and facts readily verifiable); or
     b) decline to provide an evaluative reference and refer the requester to Human Resources for a standard employment-verification response.

3. Limited private candor to protect third parties must be truthful and documented.
   - If a manager believes a departing employee would pose a genuine and significant risk to a partner or third party, the manager may communicate concerns privately to an authorized representative of the receiving organization, provided:
     a) the communication is truthful and based on documented, verifiable facts and first‑hand knowledge (no innuendo or invented claims);
     b) the communication is given only after consultation with Human Resources and, where appropriate, Legal; and
     c) the communication is documented in writing and placed in the manager’s personnel file with HR.
   - Quiet or measured phrasing and selective emphasis are permitted only to the extent they remain truthful; deliberate falsehood or fabrication is prohibited.

4. Form and authorship requirements.
   - All written references must be prepared on firm letterhead, must be dated, and must bear the printed name and handwritten signature of the manager of record.
   - If a manager has delegated the task of preparing a draft, the manager of record remains responsible for the content and must review and sign the final version.

5. Prohibition on false statements.
   - No reference, written or oral, may state anything the manager knows to be false. Fabrication, material omission intended to deceive, or intentional misrepresentation is prohibited and will be treated as a serious ethical and employment violation.

Procedure and guidance
- When asked for a reference, consult these options and use HR templates as appropriate:
  a) Positive evaluative reference (only for true, honest endorsements).
  b) Neutral verification of employment (dates, title, duties).
  c) Declination to provide evaluative reference — forward request to HR.
- If uncertain whether something may be disclosed, consult HR (and Legal where appropriate) before responding.
- Keep a copy of every signed reference and any related correspondence in the employee’s HR file.

Standards, enforcement, and discipline
- By signing below the manager acknowledges receipt of, understanding of, and agreement to comply with this policy.
- Violations of this policy (including making knowingly false statements or providing unauthorized negative disclosures) are grounds for corrective action up to and including termination.
- Human Resources will investigate complaints or allegations of noncompliance. Managers are expected to cooperate fully with investigations.

Moral rationale
- This policy reflects our obligation to be both charitable and truthful. Consistent with the Westminster teaching that honesty is a duty and lying is sinful, we will not require or condone false praise. Consistent with the duty to love our neighbor, we will refuse to gratuitously harm a departing colleague’s prospects by publicizing their faults. Where safety of others is genuinely at stake, truthful, documented, and authorized disclosure is allowed and must be handled through HR.

Both proposals as stated conflict with the Reformed rule for worship set out in the Westminster Standards. As chair and as one sworn to shepherd the church’s doctrine and worship according to Scripture and the Standards, I must propose rules that the Session can in good faith adopt and defend.

Below I therefore (A) explain the controlling teaching of the Westminster Standards in the exact words that bear on the matter, and (B) offer a warm, dignified, and binding draft “Sanctuary Arts Standards” for Session consideration that (i) keeps your mandatory liturgical items (fixed service times, printed order, approved psalter), (ii) forbids making images of the divine persons as objects of worship or directing prayer toward them, and (iii) gives clear direction about what ornamentation is permitted and what must be removed—so the Session will have an unambiguous, Scripture-shaped rule to vote on.

A. Controlling texts from the Westminster Standards (quoted exactly)

- WSC Q1 — “What is the chief end of man?”  
  A. “To glorify God, and to enjoy him for ever.”

- WSC Q2 — “What rule hath God given to direct us how we may glorify and enjoy him?”  
  A. “The Word of God, which is contained in the Scriptures of the Old and New Testament, is the only rule to direct us how we may glorify and enjoy him.”

- WSC Q99 — “Which is the second commandment?”  
  A. “The second commandment is, Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image, nor the likeness of any thing that is in heaven above, or that is in the earth beneath, or that is in the waters under the earth; thou shalt not bow down thyself to them, nor serve them: for I the LORD thy God am a jealous God, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, unto the third and fourth generation of them that hate me, And shewing mercy unto thousands of them that love me and keep my commandments.”

- WSC Q100 — “What is required in the second commandment?”  
  A. “The second commandment requireth the receiving, observing, and keeping pure and entire, all such religious worship and ordinances as God hath appointed in his Word.”

- WSC Q101 — “What is forbidden in the second commandment?”  
  A. “The second commandment forbiddeth the worshipping of God by images, or any other way not appointed in his Word.”

(These are cited because they are the Standards’ clear statements that the Word of God alone directs worship and that making images to be objects of worship, or worshipping by images, is forbidden.)

B. Draft: “Sanctuary Arts Standards” (for Session adoption; dignified, warm, and binding)

Preamble
- We adopt these Standards to honor the chief end of our lives (WSC Q1), to order all sanctuary art and ornamentation by the sole rule of Scripture (WSC Q2), and to ensure that all things in our place of worship serve gospel reverence, education in the faith, and the pure worship God requires (WSC Q100–Q101). These Standards shall be binding upon the use and alteration of the sanctuary upon Session approval and shall be incorporated into the church’s building-committee procedures for any work in the sanctuary.

Standards (binding once approved by Session)

1. Rule of Worship and Art
- All sanctuary art, ornamentation, and arrangement shall be governed by Scripture as the only rule for worship (WSC Q2) and by the principle that worship must not be conducted by images or any way not appointed in God’s Word (WSC Q100–Q101). No object, figure, carving, or installation shall be used, positioned, or treated in any way so as to be an object of worship.

2. Prohibition against images of the divine persons as objects of worship
- No sculpted, carved, painted, or pictorial representation of the Triune God (Father, Son, or Holy Spirit) shall be installed in the sanctuary as an object to which prayer or worship is directed. The Session declares this practice to be inconsistent with the second commandment and our Standards (WSC Q99, Q101).
- Accordingly, no design or placement shall be permitted (including any crucifix, sculpted “Father as an old man,” or sculpted “Spirit as a dove” intended as loci for prayer) that would present any divine Person as a representational image toward which the congregation is instructed or encouraged to kneel and pray.

3. Treatment of existing ornamentation
- The Session requires that any existing ornamentation be reviewed under the rule of Scripture and these Standards. Ornamentation that functions as an object of worship or is likely to be used as such must be removed or altered.
- However, the Session recognizes that not all carvings, stained glass, or moldings are necessarily idolatrous. Where existing stained-glass windows, carved wheat-and-vine molding, or church crosses are devotional, didactic (e.g., scriptural texts, biblical scenes used to teach Scripture), or clearly secondary to the preaching and sacramental life of the church and cannot reasonably be expected to become objects of worship, the Session may permit them to remain. The Session will make determinations case by case, guided by the prohibition in WSC Q101 and by the requirement to preserve worship according to God’s Word (WSC Q100).
- If, upon Session review, an item is judged an object of worship or likely to be used for prayer directed toward it, the Session will require its removal or alteration.

4. Prohibition of directional prayer toward images or fixed points
- The Session forbids liturgical rubrics, directions, or architectural arrangements that instruct the congregation to kneel and direct their prayers specifically toward any image, sculpture, or fixed icon. Prayers and postures are to be oriented toward God and offered according to Scripture, not toward representational objects (WSC Q100–Q101).

5. Permitted and encouraged forms of sanctuary art
- The Session warmly encourages tasteful, reverent art that teaches Scripture and points congregants to Christ without providing an object of worship. Permitted items include:
  a. Scriptural inscriptions (e.g., verse panels) that are placed to teach and focus minds on the Word.
  b. Non-figurative or symbolic art that is demonstrably devotional in the sense of pointing to biblical truth, but not pictorial representations of the divine persons intended for prayer.
  c. Craftsmanship and ornament (molding, woodwork, textiles) that are decorative and reverent, provided they are not used as aids for directing worship toward them.
- The Session will publish a brief guide (approved by majority vote) showing examples of permitted and prohibited items for the building committee’s use.

6. Liturgical continuity
- The church retains fixed service times, the printed order of worship, and the use of the approved psalter as mandatory elements of public worship. Any changes to these must be approved by Session in conformity with the Standards and the rule of Scripture (WSC Q2).

7. Decision process and appeals
- The Building Committee shall submit proposed changes to the sanctuary (installation, removal, or alteration of art/ornament) to Session with photographs, drawings, and a short statement describing the intended devotional use. Session shall decide in a stated meeting and record its reasons.
- Members may appeal a Session decision to the Presbytery under the usual rules of church government if they believe a decision contravenes the Standards.

Concluding note to Session
- These Standards are offered with a pastoral heart: to preserve Christ-centred, Word-governed worship (WSC Q1–Q2) and to avoid the very things Scripture and our Standards forbid (WSC Q99–Q101). If Session prefers a different balance (for example, a stricter prohibition that removes all figurative art, or a more permissive approach), it should do so by express minute and with explicit Scriptural and Standards-based rationale recorded.

If the Session desires, I will prepare a one-page guide with photographic examples of (A) clearly prohibited installations (e.g., sculpted triune images intended for prayer; instructions to kneel toward any image), (B) permitted examples (scripture text panels, non-figurative symbolic art), and (C) a sample submission form for the Building Committee to use in bringing proposals to Session.

Short answer up front
- Ben: Yes. As described he is keeping the Lord’s Day in the manner required by the Fourth Commandment according to the Westminster Standards: outwardly he refrains from ordinary work and devotes the day to worship and rest, and what he does that is necessary and merciful (helping a stranded motorist) is expressly permitted; inwardly he delights in the day.  
- Cara: No. By the Standards she is not keeping the Lord’s Day as required. She is engaged in ordinary, non‑necessary business during the Lord’s appointed hours and so fails the outward requirement; her sincere inward “rest” does not excuse disobedience of the express duty to abstain from ordinary labour and to attend public and private worship.

Why (the Standards behind the verdict)
- The Westminster Confession (Ch. XXI) and the Catechisms teach that the fourth commandment requires both outward observance and a right inward frame. The day is to be “sanctified” by a cessation from ordinary callings and recreations and by public and private worship, meditation, and holy fellowship. Works of necessity and mercy are explicitly excepted (they are lawful on the Lord’s Day), but ordinary worldly employments and recreations are not. The Shorter Catechism (answer on the fourth commandment) says we must rest from our own works, words, and thoughts about our worldly employments and spend the time in public and private worship, hearing God’s word, meditation, etc.
- The Standards therefore reject an exclusively inward, subjective religion that treats the Sabbath as merely an “attitude” while continuing ordinary business during the Lord’s appointed hours. Outward obedience is commanded; inward sincerity cannot supply what is commanded outwardly.

Applied to the two cases
- Ben (succeeds)
  - Outward: He keeps his store closed, attends worship, arranges his business so necessary tasks don’t bleed into the Lord’s Day, and only does what is permissibly necessary/merciful (helping a stranded motorist). That is precisely the sort of lawful exception the Standards allow. He avoids ordinary trade and inventory on the Lord’s Day. This is the pattern the Standards require.
  - Inward: He “genuinely delights” in the day and sets it apart for worship and rest. That inward delight and devotion is exactly what the Catechism commends. So both outward and inward requirements are met.
  - Pastoral note: Encourage him to continue to guard the day, to teach his household the reasons for its observance, and to take care that “mercy” does not become a cover for regular commerce.

- Cara (fails)
  - Outward: By running her cafe and personally working the morning worship hours when there is no necessity and staff could cover, she is engaging in ordinary labour and profaning the Lord’s Day according to the Standards. The exception for necessity/mercy does not apply to voluntary business activity and convenience. The Confession and Catechism require abstaining from such employments and attending public worship.
  - Inward: Sincerity and inward devotion are good and necessary, but the Standards make clear that inward frame does not nullify the outward command. Her claim that “God knows my heart” and so she may keep the Sabbath inwardly while breaking its outward duties is contrary to the teaching that both outward rest and inward sanctification are required. Thus, while she may be sincere, she is culpable for willful non‑observance.
  - Pastoral note: She should be urged to repent and to change practice: cease ordinary business on the Lord’s Day except for true necessity/mercy, attend public worship, and reorder her business so staff or scheduling can cover lawful absence if she wishes to obey the Lord’s Day.

A short pastoral application
- For Ben: Commend, encourage continued vigilance, and encourage instructing his family and employees in the duty and delight of the Lord’s Day. Be watchful that “culture” or convenience doesn’t erode his practice.
- For Cara: Gently but firmly call her to repentance and to conformity with the commandment as the church teaches it. Help her work out practical steps (staffing, schedule changes) so she can truly rest on the Lord’s Day and participate in worship. Offer to study the biblical and confessional teaching with her and to obtain counsel from her elders if she is in a church.

Whereas this congregation’s Session is bound by its sworn subscription to the Westminster Standards and must order public worship according to the Word of God and the principles set forth therein (Westminster Confession of Faith, ch. 1; ch. 21), the Session hereby adopts the following Reverent Worship Standards to preserve worship that is godly, orderly, and free from innovation. These standards are issued by the Session for the good of the congregation and, pursuant to the Session’s rule and oversight, are binding in every public service of worship of this church until further action of the Session.

In adopting these rules the Session affirms the Confession’s teaching that we must worship God only in ways He has appointed (WCF 21), that the sacraments appointed by Christ (baptism and the Lord’s Supper) are the seals and pledges of the covenant (WCF 27, 29; Larger Catechism), and that no new rite, ceremony, or outward practice may be introduced as a means of securing or assuring a person’s standing before God.

Accordingly, and by the authority of the Session, the following are hereby required.

1. Covenant Renewal before the Benediction
a. The Session forbids the introduction or requirement of any new sacramental rite, token-laying, or bodily act that claims to effect, renew, or secure a member’s standing before God. In particular, no mandated practice shall be instituted that asserts that the physical presentation of an object (whether a token, badge, or other device) operates to “seal,” “renew,” or maintain a member’s covenant standing in the manner of a sacrament.
b. To encourage corporate remembrance of God’s covenant mercies, each Sunday immediately before the benediction a brief corporate Covenant Renewal shall be observed. This shall consist of:
   - A concise exhortation or Scripture reading (led by the minister or designated leader), and
   - A single, brief corporate prayer of covenant renewal and dedication.
   The act is devotional and confessing in nature and is explicitly not a sacrament; nothing in the prayer or exhortation shall state or imply that any external object or outward act confers or secures saving grace or covenant status.
c. Personal devotional tokens, when kept by members as private reminders of baptismal vows or membership, are permitted as private mementos. Such items shall never be required for public worship nor taught as necessary to one’s covenant standing. Failure to participate in the corporate Covenant Renewal does not nullify or “unseal” a member’s standing; membership and covenant standing remain in Christ and are subject to the Word, the sacraments, and the ordinary discipline of the Church.

2. Orderly, Reverent Behavior during Singing and Prayer
a. Public worship shall be conducted in the fear of God, with inward devotion and outward decency and order (WCF 21). Members and visitors are required to conduct themselves so as to promote reverence and avoid distraction.
b. Therefore, during congregational singing and prayer, members shall refrain from demonstrative, theatrical, or ostentatious bodily displays that draw attention from the Word and prayer. Specifically, raising hands in a demonstrative posture, waving, swaying in a way that causes distraction, clapping, shouting, or other outward gestures intended as expressive display are prohibited in the sanctuary during the public worship service.
c. This prohibition is not a denial that worship engages the heart and affections (which the Session affirms); rather it is to preserve an atmosphere of reverent, ordered worship where the Word, the preaching, prayer, and the sacraments are central. Quiet, modest posture and appropriate stillness are required. Pastors and elders will teach the biblical principles of worshipful affections and will receive any overt displays pastorally and patiently; persistent willful breach will be addressed by pastoral counsel and, if necessary, ecclesiastical discipline.

3. Time and Order of Services
a. Public Sunday worship shall begin at 10:00 a.m. on the Lord’s Day and shall be conducted in a fixed, printed order of service approved by the Session.
b. The ordinarily anticipated length of the service is seventy (70) minutes. The Session recognizes that occasionally the service may extend (for sacramental occasions, funerals, special teaching, etc.), but leaders shall endeavor to keep the service within the stated time by prudent planning and faithful discipline of the order.
c. The printed order of service shall include the essential elements of public worship as taught in the Standards: Scripture readings, prayer, preaching of the Word, singing, and the sacraments as appointed. Any liturgical texts or additions must be approved by the Session and must be consistent with the Word and our Confessional standards.

4. Decorum in the Sanctuary and Care of Young Children
a. No beverages (including coffee), food, or open containers shall be brought into the sanctuary during the public worship service. This rule is to preserve cleanliness, avoid distraction, and maintain reverence. Exceptions (e.g., for medical need) may be granted by the pastor on request.
b. Children under the age of six shall ordinarily be cared for in the nursery during the public worship service unless the Session, after due consideration of the child’s age and maturity and the needs of the family and congregation, makes an exception. The Session directs the elders and teaching staff to provide biblically faithful, well-supervised nursery care and to assist parents in training children for worship as they grow.
c. Parents remain responsible for the behavior of their children and are encouraged to use the nursery when it best serves the family and the congregation. Pastoral counsel and resources will be provided to help families bring children under godly discipline and prepare them for corporate worship.

5. Approved Psalter and Hymnal Repertoire
a. Congregational singing shall be taken only from the Session-approved psalter-and-hymn list. The Session shall approve and publish the list and may add or remove items only by Session vote after careful review for biblical fidelity and doctrinal soundness.
b. The Session requires that all sung material be theologically consistent with Scripture and the Westminster Standards. Music chosen shall be conducive to congregational singing, edifying, and reverent.
c. Musical leadership shall ensure that arrangements and instrumental accompaniment serve the congregation’s singing and do not draw undue attention to performers.

6. Oversight and Enforcement
a. The Session, under Christ, is responsible to oversee and enforce these standards. Ministers, elders, and designated worship leaders are charged to teach these standards, to model them, and to apply them pastorally.
b. Ushers and leaders shall courteously remind worshipers of these standards when needed. Persistent or willful refusal to conform after patient pastoral admonition may be referred for church discipline in accordance with the Session’s usual practice and constitutional procedures.
c. The Session will review these standards annually and may amend them as it deems necessary, always in fidelity to the Word and the Westminster Standards.

Conclusion
These standards are enacted to foster worship that honors God, guards the congregation from unlawful innovations, and promotes holiness and edification in the body. They seek neither cold formality nor unregulated emotion, but worship in spirit and truth in the beauty of holiness (WCF 21). By the Session’s authority, they are effective immediately for all public worship services unless and until revised by the Session.
